From all I can hear the new Education Code is not likely to lead to anything in the nature of a :set debate in the House. It is recognised that the alterations made are mainly on points of detail,and that in most cases they are improvements. There will be a general discussion on these points upon the estimates, but from the teacher's point of view no serious question is likely to be raised. The National Union has, however, one important griev- ance which will be ventilated at all events in Com- mittee of Supply. This is in regard to the provi- sions dealing with the number of children whom each teacher is to be hereafter qualified to teach. It is complained that these will bear harshly upon some of the poorer Voluntary schools. Apart from the provisions of the Code,the friends of the Volun- tary schools intend to renew their campaign on the Estimates in regard to the administrative action of the Education Department. They protess to ac- cept Mr. Acland's promises of indulgent treatment as far as he is concerned, but they complain that the matter is really in the hands of the inspectors, and that the inspectors are doing their best at the present time to make life a burden to the managers of the Voluntary schools.

I understand that Mr. Havelock Wilson and the members acting with him are highly delighted at the promise made by the President of the Board of Trade of an inquiry into the question of under- manning. Mr. Wilson claims that he has been agita- ting for such an inquiry or fifteen years. There is no doubt that Mr. Mundella has gone further even than the seamen's representatives had ven- tured to hope.

Quite a number of African hunters and explorers were present on Tuesday evening at ',he meeting of the Zoological Society, the attractions being a paper by Captain Gwyne on the game animals of Somali- land, and another by Mr. Coryndon on the white rhinoceros of South Africa. Mr. Coryndon lately shot two of these very rare beasts in the north- eastern portion of Mashonaland, and one of them, a fine bull fully grown, has been secured by the British Museum. The hide of the other has been purchased by Mr. Rothschild for his museum at Tring, while it is hoped to secure the skeleton for the Museum of Zoology at Cambridge. This huge animal, the largest of terrestrial mammals after the elephant, will, according to Mr. Selous, in the course of the next few years become absolutely extinct, only one small herd, it is believed, being left in Mashonaland. Some idea of the size of those shot by Mr. Coryndon may be formed when it is stated that each of them was estimated to be equal in bulk to two of the largest Clydesdale horses. Mr. Coryndon is leaving England shortly to return to the Zambesi country with a view to adding to our knowledge of its fauna.

The Liberals are very well satisfied with the re- sult of the Romford election, but they believe that in more fortunate circumstances it might have been still better. lam told that if thy had had another week to hunt up the removals the result would have been different. A large body of the electors did not go to the poll. One cause of this abstention is to be found in the fact that a great body of the gas stokers, who are Liberals almost to a man, have just left the constituency to work in the brickfields, as they do in the spring. There is no doubt that the breakdown of the Great Eastern Railway ser- vice prevented many of the out-votets from getting to Romford in time, and the Conservatives claim that that helps to account for the diminution in the majority. Both sides are agreed that for some days past Romford has been " swimming in beer," though how far anyone is to be held responsible for this in the case of a great brewery town i•=, of course, open to question. We shall perh..ps hear more upon this subject.

No seriou3 importance is attached either in Liberal or Nationalist quarters to the resolutions passed at the Redtriondite Convention or to the ex- travagant vapourings of the " Irish Independent." Two causes are thought to be at work. Iu the first place there has been during the past yeat an un- settlement of feeling in Ireland which has detached many Nationalists from the official party, possibly because of unfortunate displays of want of unity. The Redroondites are angling desperately for the class whom Americans effectively describe as " dis- gruntled " politicians. liii Irish reforms come more to the ,fr,rit again, and while dissensions are rife among Nationalist leaders, the opportunity is too favourable not to be worked for all it is worth. In the next place it has been more than once rlui- pected that tne Redniondite faction were making bids more or less open for a Tory alliance. That the present display of fury end unreason and de- monstrations of distrust towards the Government are in one sense overtures to Mr. Balfour is obvious.

In this connection it is to the initiated unneces- sary, but to the world outside Westminster it may be usef ul,to state that the absence of Irish National- ists on Monday was partly owing to the serious inconvenience of recommencing the session on a Monday, and partly owing to the conviction,which turned out to be well-founded, that no division could or would be taken tilt Thursday. There is not the slightest reason to think that any of the lfationalists are disposed to risk the existence of the (4overnment by absenting themselves, or that there is any covert sympathy with the Redtnondite professions of hostility. Indeed most people treat. the latter as merely meant forlrish consumption, and expect to see the Rtdmondites in the Government lobby on the first really critical occasion.

Major Ralph Egerton, who hasjust been promoted has risen from the ranks. He it was who saved the colours of th 4 94th Regiment during the-Boer war in 1881. Although wounded... he wrapped the col- ours around him and carried them forty miles through a. closely-guarded country to Pretoria. For this he was given a commission, and since then has been on duty at Cape Coast Castle and Jamaica.

And this is one of her baby soliloquies : Nurse is very clever At her daily toil; But at night she wakes me up And gives me castor oil. Castor oil is hateful ; What I like the most Is the cheerful nursery tea And the buttered toast.
This, the _Express remarks, would not bring the blush of shame to the most modest.

The ladies who have resolved to be Volunteers have decided that their costume shall be tunic; knickers, stockings, and short gaiters, of which the colour shall be blue, not too dark. Scotland-yard has unofficially informed the ladies that they are not likely to be arrested for conning the proposed dress so long as none of them attempt to personate men. There is certainly a splendid time in store for the London street by. The Lord Mayor, too, must not forget our Amazons; they will make a splendid adjunct to the annual show.

Count Tolstoi has been " interviewed " by a Bus- eian journalist, and told him that patriotism is inconsistent with Christianity. Yet surely this Russian Grand Old Man has heard of an English- man whose name was General Gordon. But the Count draws a fine distinetion—so tine that many people with a less acute moral eyesight will not be able to discover, wherein the difference lies. For Count Tolstoi, while objecting to patriotism, is yet by no means adverse to "national self-love" He gave much credit to the Americans for possessing this quality, and certainly with them " patriotism ' or "national self-love" is a very positive quality.

• The count tells an interesting story of this in- tense feeling on the part of our cousins across the Atlantic. "I one day wrote an article," he says, "on America and the Americans, in which I did not particularly overload the latter with flattery. Nevertheless, I sent the MSS. over the ocean, thinking it would be accepted by any paper as eagerly as my other productions. Not a bit of it. The translator took it to fourteen different editors without getting it accepted, and finally it bad to be sent to England."

The Queen has sixty pianos at Osborne, Windsor, and Buckingham Palace. Many of them are hired. Lady Brooke has about twenty small Japanese spaniels worth one hundred pounds each. Mr. E. Brough has twenty bloodhounds worth three hundred pounds each Two if these dogs were used in looking tor " Jack the Ripper." In the White Drawing Room at Buckingham Palace is the famous ivory grand, so called becaut..e the top is wholly covered with a thin, unbroken sheet of ivory, which was uncurled as it were from one enormous tusk. This priceless instrument is also decorated with some beautiful and delicate Vernis-Martin work, which was originally on a harpsichord that belonged to Anna of Austria.

Crystallization of Grasses. This can be done by making a strongsolution of alum, and then inserting the article. It will crystallize not only grasses, but pieces of coke or baskets made of cane or wire. In the case of baskets, cover the parts with different coloured thread or worsted ; by this m ,ans the crystals will appear coloured according to taste. For the same purpose, sulphate of copper, sulphate of iron, or bichroroate of potass may be used (each having a different form of crystal and different colour) but alum is preferable. The size of crystal is regulated by the temperature of the solution at the time of inserting the article.

The American Speaker's Courtship. The wife of the American Speaker has set a curious example to other ladies placed in similar positions. Mrs. Crisp has been interviewed by a representative of the " Philadelphia Times," and the good woman, who is a " confirmed invalid," has been telling a reporter how she fell in love with " Charlie." Crisp in his youthful days must have been a gallant young spark, for he carried off the Southern belle from under the very noses of her parents. When Mrs. Crisp's mother heard the news that her " da'ater " had eloped with Charlie she fell ill and went to bed. After many days a level-headed sister sent a letter to the runaways and they returned. Mrs. Crisp went to her mother's bedroom, and the following pathetic scene ensued :—" She lay back among her pillows, and I threw myself on the bed by her side,weep- ing, begging her to forgive me. My sister, who was in the room, joined in my prayer, and in a few moments my mother had me in her arms, and we were all three smiling through happy tears. In a few moments my father came in, and taking in at a glance the state of affairs, steppe(' out to the gate and brought in Mr. Crisp to join the family grolp." It is quite too awful to con- jure up any such revelations about the early days of Mr. Peel.
Girls and Household Dutie,s.

How contemptible it is, says a lady writer in the "Newcastle Weekly Chronicle," to hear young girls say they never do this or wouldn't do that, meaning little houserold duties! I never hear this kind el conversation without wishing I could do something dreadful to those who make the remarks. Girls who pride themselves on never doing anything except read, talk, paint, or play one or other musical instrument, are poor tools indeed. But when the remark is made by a chit of sixteen or eighteen years, and in such a manner as o lead you to suppose that all who do assist in household work are lowering themselves, it makes me boil with iage and contcmi7t. For such narrow-minded pe.ople I would like to qticAe tho hours and duties of the wife of Edward VI. and mother of the Queen of Henry VII., which is culled from a book edited and revised by Lady Colin Campbell : Hese at four o'clock, and helped Catherine to milk the cows. Six o'clock, breakfasted; the buttock of beef too much boiled, and the beer a little of the stalest. Seven, went to walk with the lady my mother in the courtyard. Ten, went to dinner. Eleven, rose from the table, the company all desirous of walking into the fields. Four, went to prayers. Six, fed the hogs and poultry. Seven, supper on the table. Nine o'clock—the company fast asleep—these late hours are very disagreeable. I really believe that it is when yalune men are in cen- venation with the type of girl mentioned above that they are afraid to think of taking unto themselves a wile. Every day brings with it the certainty that the men of the present day are very chary about marriage. Girls are not educated—at least some of them—to under- take the mara4ement of a house, or to learn to economise in the least. They are brought up-in an extravagent style, and are allowed to lead aimless, lazy lives, which utterly disables them to take charge of a house, unless provided with an unlimited income. And so young WI e fight shy of them.

CHAPTICIt VI!. THE YOUNG WINGS LONG TO FLY. The same fond mother bent at night O'er each fair sleeping brow; She had each folded flower in sight. Ms. HEIWANS The shadow that had swept so suddenly over the Soul of the Lady Beatrice disappeared as suddenly before the sunshine of the happy faces around her She could not cherish sad thoughts or forebodings lon in that pleasant atmosphere. lhe meal proceeded, enlivened with mirth and cheerful conversation, until the Lady Beatrice said,

smiling : "We will go back to the drawing-room " She arose, and the signal was acted upon by the others. They returned to the drawing-room, where the mother became the bright centre of attraction, her children clustering around her, and her hus-
band seating himself beside her. - "This a 'delightful coming home ! " she said, apparently forgetful that every week witnessed a similar scene. "To-morrow shall be a holiday.

No lessons for the children, no teaching for papa. We will have a picnic in the conservatory, and, if it is pleasant, walks and frolics in the garden." This programme excited general approbation. The count, versed in all the polite and solid ac- complishments of the present day, chose to beguile his many solitary hours by becoming himself the principal instructor of his children. Besides the pleasure he derived in shaping and cultivating their minds and hearts himself, he had another reason for acting as their tutor. It was out of the question to send them to school, and no resident governess or tutor could be ad- Mitted to the Evergreens to become a spy upon the family secrets. The modern languages, especially Bpani3h—to keep up the necessary fiction of his Castilian birth—music, dancing, and the solid branches of their native tongue, were carefully taught by the count to his apt pupils, and the con- • MITIZhco was that they knew more than most school bred children, besides possessing self-confidence and self-reliance, qualities their father had taken special care to cultivate in his daughter and elder

The newest shades of green are either very pals or dark emerald; a bile, again, the colour known as chartreuse is gaining popularity. A pretty gown, in the latter tint, lia.s the shape of the skirt parti- cularly good, being of sufficient fulness over the feet, yet fitting round the hips with glove-like tightness. A trimming of jet passementerie bands the skirt three times, and is repeated on the bodice as an outline to the vaudyked yoke awl quaintly-cut shoulder frill, both of which are of black velvet. A folded band of velvet circloAs the neck, and fastens at the back, but the waistband should be of the same shade as the dress. The novel sleeves &low a loose sling-shaped upper part, while the under-sleeve may be either of black ye vet throughout, or of the green cloth cuffed with velvet.

It would be quite possible to buy an absolutely plain and even unlined cape of plain cloth or tweed and then braid it or line it at home. Braid may now be purchased so very inexpensively by the dozen yards, and short lengths of shot and fancy silks may be picked up for such very trifling sums that the cost of these additions to our capes need not be very alarming. At any rate, l present the idea for what it is worth, and hope that many will succeed in carrying it out. A thick fur edged cape may be completely transformed for spring and summer wear by removing the fur, carefully brushing and ironing, and finally braiding with braid that should be either a match or a contrast. As to the lining, this is easily managed. Cat to the required size, and slip-stitch the silk to tho cloth down each front and along the bottom. If only a very short length of silk be at hand, face only the front parts of the cape with this, making the silk reach as far as possible on either side, then turn in the raw edge, and catch it doyn lightly to he cloth.

Feathers are also much used on spring millinery, particularly ostrich tips; indeed, these can never be said to be out of season from January to Decem- ber, but a novelty in this line is the fashion of powdering such tips with fine cut jet., and the elect is magical, and the hitherto somewhat funereal appearance of the black ostrich feather is now no more.

A large hat looks better worn with a cape than a small bonnet, which is apt to make the wearer look insignificant with so much width on the shoulders. A pretty model is made of black velvet, trimmed with tips, and a brntht-eoloured rosette set under the brim.

What to wear at dinner when in deep mourning is always a difficalt ques ion, but it is solved by a dull black grenadine Empire tea gown, over black satin, which fits the figure perfectly, the over dress being, however, loose. Stole ends are intro- duced on coats and on bodices, and one lhus arranged entirely enveloped the figure. But the novel point was a loose oblong piece, like the tabard of a herald falling from the bust to below the waist. It was made in fawn-coloured cloth, finely worked in jet. A pretty tweed not too seve,rely Quat,er-like is difficult to find; but a pink shot with brown, of a velvet-like softness on its surface, had particular m rrits. It had a Figaro jacket, yellow lace falling in the front, lined with gold, and inside the skirt was a balaycuse of alternate pink and gold bouillonne3.

131ain skirts will this season be trimmed at the edge, and a very handsome Parisian model of faille Franga-se in dull fawn had a nine-inch border of moss-green Velvet, over which, nob quite reaching to the lower edge, came a broad open-patterned guipure in a deep ecru tint. Vandykes of jet, with the straight edge upwards, are used in this same fashion, as, for instance, pa e grey silk, green, darker grey velvet, and jet vandylra.

A pretty model has the full skirt absolutely plain. The three faint lines round the foot hem, and repeated aga n round the knees, are obtained by machine-stitchi-g, which gives a smait and very .1 " tailor-made " appearance to this pretty gown. The tight-fitting bodice is arranged to button over ' on the left side, and the deep full basque does not meet in the centre by some fourteen incues. The wide ravers need some care in making. They must be faced with cloth, interlined with tailors' canvas, and then machine-stitched round three times. The sleeve cuffs and hasque are finished in the same moznen.
Yours as ever.
Jastint.

"The hour is late," said the Lady Beatrice, at last, as the clock struck. "It is time that such young eyes were cltmed in sloop. We will sing our evening hymn, and then you shall all re- tiro."

Giralda went to the piano and began to play the customary hymn. The three fresh sweet young voices bore up the words on streams of melody, and the count and the Lady Beatrice gave depth and tone to the music. The hymn concluded, the count offered up the evening prayer, and the young people gathered around to bid their parents good night. "I will put Fay to bed as usull," said the Lady Beatrice, taking the hand of her youngest darling In her own. My baby has not grown beyond my care yet." Rupert approached his mother, kissed her, and whispered: "Mamma, can I see you alone a little while to- night?" The Lady Beatrice looked at him earnestly, somethinc, in his tones arresting her attention. He seemed Coss boyish than usual. A look of high resolve shone from his dark eyes, and there was a strangely resolute curve about his month. His manner was earnest, and full of sudden and half suppressed agitation. I will Come to your room, Rupert, as soon as Fay has retired," she said, with affectionate in- torest.

The lad stepped back, giving place to his sister. " Mamma, whispered Giralda, " I must see you alone in the morning. Will you save an hour for me?" "Yes, darling. You shall have my first hour after breFiliast. You will find me in papa's study." Giving her daughter a kiss, the Lady Beatrice retired with her younger son, escorting 'him to his room. She put him to bed herself, not leaving him until she had seen his fair head pillowed for the ni;ht. Then closing the violet eyes with kisses, she passed into the chamber of Rupert. -

He waa sitting by a little table upon which was a eandle dimly burning. There were books all around him, on the tables, in the little bookcase, on the hanging shelves, even littering the pretty, white bed. Pictures adorned the walls, and below them were rows of insects pinned to the wall, and bearing elaborate descriptions in Latin, illustrating , Ruperes mania for natural history. A little glued. ' cabinet exhibited a fine collection of minerals. In- terspersed with these evidences of grarve pursuits were balls and bats, fishing-rods, skates, and similar material for pastime's. Rupert arose at the entrance of his mother, leading her to the chair he had occupied. Then he flung himself at her feet, burying his face in her lap. "What is the matter, my son !" asked the Lady Beatrice, anxiously. " You are not ill ?" " Oh, no, mamma," he answered, trying to speak cheerfully, hut failing lamentably in the effort. "I am well enough. I want to talk to you about myself. I am almost fifteen years old. Have you formed any plans for my future?" A look of keen anxiety passed over her lady- shisp's face, and she threaded her fingers through her son's dusky locks without replying, .The hour she had so long dreaded had come. Rupert's ardent young soul had awaLened to the stern realities of fife. "Am I to be a lawyer, a clergyman, or a doctor, mother? Or am Ito learn a business?" The Lady Beatrice lifted her head proudly, her haughty English prejudices fired by :these simple questions. "My son earn his living !" she exclaimed. "My husband's sou to work for his bread? Rupert, what strange ideas arc working in your brain ? " The boy lifted his head. A scarlet glow burned on, either cheek. His eyes were full of earnest "Mother !" he said, gravely, dropping in his earnestness the pretty pet name by which he almost always called her, •NA hy should not your son earn his own living? Why should not your husband's son work for his bread.? lam hearty and strong, old beyond my years. Is it worse for my father's son to work than my father's wife ? "

"Hush, Rupert," said the Lady Beatrice, grave- ly, her eyes drooping, her cheeks rivaling his own. "Do you not sec that your wards imply blame to papa? No one must blame him —least- of all, his children. He is the noblest an grandest of men. Thera is a necessity which keeps me from you all a portion of the time, my son. have' told you truly—l am an actress! 11tit the theatre in which I play, and the name I bear within it, my children Cannot ;:now for the present. * The time will come when they shall hear the whole story. Till then, Rupert, be patient." ' • "I do uot blame my father," returned Rupert, his eyes filling with tears. "He works, too, at his books. He has made money in publishing them, and has another almost ready for the press. He teaches us, andolie is the moat, generous of fathers, the kindest and tonderest of friends. But, mamma, I feel that I must do something! I cannot always be dependent upon your and papa's earnings. I imagine that poor papa is not wealthy. If he was, he would. not let you wOrk so!" "Papa has plenty of money, Rupert," said the Lady Beatrice. "Whatever you desire you may have. Would you like an increase of spending money? Or do you want apparatus for experiments, or a new stock of books ? ' and she glanced around the pretty chamber. , "No,- mother. My puree is full now. I fancied that papa was a Spanish refugee,, with buta scanty fortune. Ido not want to do anything you would net like, but, if I had my wish, f should like above all things to go to a public school, and afterwards to a university." • Having thus unburdened his 'heart of its most secret aspirations, Rupert buried his face again in the lap of the Lady Beatrice, and.awaited in breath- less silence her reply. ,It came at last, sweet, clear; and, the boy ,honght, tbactured*with sadnes.. "What, are -you tired of the home-nest, my

" Oh, no, no, indeed, a,' was the quick and . passionate response. 'Houle is the sweetest. place in all- the world, But, ,mother, the young eagles do not stay always in the nest. They imam to fly out, and then come-back again • to rest, you know. I have read the lives of 'many of England's great men. I feel as if I had it in me to be a states- man by and by, just as Fay will be a' poet" "I think you have," said the Lady •Beatrice, thoughtfully. ; The boy grew flushed and eager at this unex- pected confirmatlon of his dreams from such a source. "I want tG :.:rcat for your sake," he whis•

pered. "And then, when my Tame Mat its bright- -1 1 ,it, I will say, as many a great man has said: ' owe it all to my mother.'" 1.. The Lady Beatrice drew her son closer to her t bosom, smiling tenderly at his enthusiasm, and said :

"I have been expecting that you would soon begin to feel your strength, Rupert; that, like the young birds, you would soon want to try yonr winqs. lam not prepared with an anawer to- night. I must talk the matter over with your father. But in answer to your question about your future, I can set your mind at rest now. You are your father's heir, and if you live, will be called upon, in due course of time, to bear a proud title, to give lustre to a grand old name. You will have estates and tenantry, and be a great landed pro- prietor." Rupert looked at his mother in wondering aston- ishment.

"This communication must be kept a strict se- cret," said her ladyship. "Say nothing even to Giralda of what I have told you. You shall be sent to a university either here or abroad in due time. You must have faith and patience, my son. Remember that a brilliant future is before you." "Yes mother l" exclaimed the still wondering boy. "Has papa lands and tenantry ?" "I cannot answer you now, my son. You shall know all in good time. You must trust in your parents, and believe they will consider your best good- " I will—l do !" cried the boy eagerly. "I am quite content now, since you know my hopes and wishes. The life you say will be mine is the one I covet most. To have leisure to cultivate my tastes, to travel and to study, with money to ure as I will, with tenantry to care for and elevate, with a public career open to me—this will be per- fect happiness to me. It seems as if I must have been made for such .a life." "You certainlylave been educated for it," re- sponded the I ady Beatrice. "Riches and a high. position bring with them great responsibilities. You have been carefully trained to meet those responsibilities wisely and ably. That you may use the wealth and influence that you will some day inherit, so that the world will be the beqter for your having lived in it, Rupert, is my hope and prayer. You will have time, money, position and influenae, and can direct your ambition in any way you choose. Ambition is a good thing, Ru- pert ;_ only let it be a noble one. Let your aims be grand and exalted. You can be a statesman—" • "But mother, lam the son of a foreigner." " You are English born, my boy. That is enough," said her ladyship, with a smile. " -We have talked sufficiently for ,o-night, and it is time for you to go to bed. " Remember all I have, confided to you with religious care. , We can re- sume our conversation to-morrow, without dan- ger of making you sleepless." She embraced him with all a mother's pride and tenderness, her heart secretly exulting over his noble young soul and rising ambitibia, and then she took her departure, leaving with the lad new aspirations' new hopes, and new dreams. The hall was dimly lighted as she came out, from Ilupert'e chamber. The lower part of the. dwelling was enshrouded in darkness. She went into her daughter's room, but Giralda was wrapped in sweet, girlish slumbers. Breathing a blessing upon tier lovely first- born child, the Lady Beatrice went on to the study. Her Ines'aand was waiting for her there, seated on the tiger-skin couch by the fireside. The count - opened his arms to his wife. She sank into, them, and leaned uptm his breast with a pleasant sense of restfulness.' "What did Rupert 'want?" asked her husband, after a brief silence. "To try his wings, as the young eagles do," an- swered the wife, between smiling and sighing. "The hour we have foreseen for our son is come. my husband, and sooner ;ban we expected. He wants to know what his future is to be, and if he may not be sent to a. public school and a univer- aity." - "I wish we could have kept Rupert a child a . while longer," said the count, gravely. "1 know that his training has developed him early, but I would like to keep our children sirnply children a long while yet. How can we send him from its without exposing him to insults and wronos? lie will tie looked down upon because his mother is supposed to be an actress. Or he may learn by some strauge chance that she is not the kind of actress he has been led to believe, and he may be- lieve he has reason to blush for his parentage. I 1. have enemies—Lord Trevelyan and Lord Adlowe-= who, did' they but suspect the boy's 'paternity, would delight to torture my soul through my spir- ited son. Worse, they would track me out, and have me arrested on the old charge, and thus cover you and our children with shame and ignominy. We must guard our children closely, Beatrice. We must guard our children closely, Beatrice. We must guard our secret with our lives." Again a chill crept over the Lady. Beatrice. " Your words frighten me, my husband," she said, with a troubled look. "We will keep our children within the four walls of home. Rupert must wait until our path is clear. You spoke of being tracked! Who shall track you o„tit ? . Every one '7l)k...lit:yes you dead. Your indentity is care- , fully hidden. You are known in this neighbour- hood as the Spanish refugee and author. No cue can penetrate under that disguise." " Adlowe is very keen Beatrice. Suppose he were to follow you here ?" "I will red on He my vigilancerand guard against snob a fearful poosi bifity. I will perfect my dis- guise. No, my husband, let us fear nothing, but trust in that Providence which has so far cherished us !" and the Lady Beatrice resolutely shock off her gloom. We can live for years to come, if neces- sary, as we have doue. for years past. Should we ever deem such a course advisable, we can send Ru- pert to a German University." "We will (io so if nothing occurs th. year to re- lieve us," replied the count. " I have waited year alter year tor that something to occur, and !Qat for you my lifc.mnst have lyconie a burden to me. As it is, I have had more than my share of joy anti lnippiness. To yen .owe it, Beatrice, that my cup of bliss is running over." .lie called her tender and loving names, blessing. her for her faith, her love, her hope, her trust. And, nestling in that loving breast, encirchaA by arms that bore up their burden proudly, the Lady' •. Bcatriee felt how Sweet a thin,/ is life—what a glorious thing is existence ! In her happy tense of security, she could then have defied Lord Adlowe —defied the vindictive Marquis Tievelan—deilud the world

div.head: PA RISII REGISTERS.
div.p: PA RISII REGISTERS.

The House of Commons has to consider the question . whether the parochial clergy are to continue to be the custodians of the Parish Registers, whether the &regi- ments are to become the property of the District or ! Parish Councils, or whether, like so many of them, in- cluding al the Nonconformist ones prior to 1837, they are to be removed to the Public Record 0:Bee, or to Somerset House. In view of this, the following facts about Parish Registers will bs of some interest at the present moment : The history of these Registers proves at once that those who insist that they are public property, and their op- ponents. whe, quite as positively, pronounce then* church documents, are equally wrong—if their conten- tions are to be accepted in an exclusive sense. They be- gan by being simply labours of love on the part of the clergy, and after many years received partial recogni- tion as public documents. In early times, the Monastic- Registers—priceless records, of which toe many were scattered during the fanaticism which (tarried every- thing before it between the suppression of monasteries, and the re-erganisation of the church—supplied the plane of the Parish Registers. But as the deaths registered I were as a rule only those of important persons, the oh- ject being to tell when masses were due, their value is , limited. Even when a wider range was taken, only the I families of founders; benefactors, and the like were I taken notice of in the necrologies. Ordinary folk in I those ages, and long subsequent)y, contented them- selves with private records, or with entering the births,. deaths, and marriages of their family on the fly-leaf of a. family Bible, or, when Bibles were scarce, on the blank pages of books of devotion. In 1538 Thomas Cromwell ordained that regular Parish Register should be kept in order to meet the needs created by the suppression of religious houses. This injunction, however, WAS carried out So carelessly that in 1597 Elizabeth ordered, not only that the Regis- ters should be better kept, but that copies should be sent to the Bishops. During the • Commonwealth the Regis- ters again fell into irregularity, and on the Restoration it was found that many of them were lost, probably' having been destroyed, through the ignorance or the iconocalism of the " Registers " who, from 1633 to 1660, had been elected to keep them. After the Restoration, the Parish Registers began t) become more interesting, and even entertaining. They contain notices ot a host Of events, lay as well as ecclesiastical, in addition to the, usual entries of births, deaths, and marriages. These records were not compulsory. The Nonconformists,not to speak of the " Fieet parsons," who officiated in pub- • lic houses, kept their own Registers. But the funerals. of Roman Catholics and Dissenters were often noted in the Church Registers, which thus became fairly full re- cords el the simple annals of the trnelish Parishes. It was not until 1812 that the Registers again attracted the attention of Parliament. The paucity of the entries in them was becoming notorious, while the neg- lect of the incumbents and Bishops in seeing that they were properly ,kept, and the old ones ipreserved from mutilation and decay, was even then scandalous. Otte* they lay in the church, open to any one who chose to examine them, without due care being taker., ingainst an improper use being made of the liberty. In other cases, the parson's library was where these ancient chronicles were kept. The result was what might have been expected. Many of these records vanished for- ever, having perished in parsonages fires, or in the nts which overtoek the churches. Quite as frequently they were lost, or stolen, or used tor lighting fires or covering jem-pots. Still more frequently they were mu'ilated for criminal purposes. The ignorant parish sexton was often bribed, or hoodwinked when. deep in the ale pot,into permitting an entry to be altered a page cut out, or a volume borrowed, by a plausible visitor, in order that a birth, a marriage, or a death, might be unproved or proved, to suit the pilferer's pur- poses. Such abuses furnished a favourite plot to the olller novelists, and the state of the Registers shows clearly enough that such devices were not uncommon. The earliest Registers are extremely rare, and even those of the eighteenth century are very imperfect. As few of the missing ones had been transcribed,these losses are irreparable. In 1801, it was discovered that out Of eleven thousand parishes in England, only eight hundred and twelve Registers, datine from 1538, were srill iii existence. The returns in 1834 have to admit that eves that small remnant had decreased, from causes over which the custodians had in most cases perfect control. Accordeig to one authoritv, 'there are now more than a hundred Essex parishes which have lost all their registers down to the time of the Civil War, In IEII2 tee Regis- ters were ordered to be better kept, arranged, and pre- served, and the names in them to be alphabetically indexed.

Sig cc 1837, when Registration becamg.comptilsory,the Parish Regicters have been of purely ecclesiastical mom- ent, though on that account, if intelligently kept, they, are not l,ss necessary to the local historian. But in many cases the most culpable ignorance of their value has been exhibited. Now-a-days, we would fain hope- that this is exceptional, and that the clergymen who either refuse to give au excerpt from the Registers, neg- lect to take any notice of applications to that effect,. demaod exorbitant fees for doing so, or are unable to decipher the old caligraphy, are rare examples of rude- lieSS goil lack of intelligence. Many are, on the contrary only too pr.ud to see the local re7.urds made use of, and refuse to charge any fee for the trouble of searching them in the interest of literary men, private pedigree makers, or solicitors. This they have no right to be- called upon to do. There is a legal scale of charges— not hi2h, tint fair—for such services, and this payment being tendered, the law has a remedy for the custodians neglect el a public function. In short, if the Parish Ralords, are not to be removed to Fetter Cane or Som- erset fl, use, ParliiJnent should not abandon thens to the ri,k it fire or the pr inks of children, the carelessness of I • • housemaids, or the knavery of the world at large. A roomy safe ought, at least, to be added to the vestry furniture.

The question of a deputation attending the con- gress was of very' little importance to him, but the de- putation in question was in his opinion the most impor- tant of any connected with the Council. Only the mover and seconder voted for it, and 17 voted for the confirmation of the minutes, the resolution being thus carried by a large majority. SANITARY WORKS COMMITTEE.—MORE DEPUTATIO*S. The minutes of this Committee stated that Couneillor ,Shillcock was appointed a member of the Longford Sub. Committee in place of the late Councillor Bonnell. The estimated expenditure for the Committee was £8.41319-. The minutes contained the results of Mr. Alfred Smetharn's analysis of a certain sample of manure which he says closely resembles the better kinds of Peruvian guano, and there can be no doubt that if properly used it will be found to be an exceedingly valuable fertilizer. Councillor MONKS moved the confirmation of the minutes of the Committee, and referred to the estimate, giving reasons in detail for the increases. He said thst during the coming year they only proposed to spend what was the average normal sum required to carry on Longford, which was between £2.600 and £2,700. That had been so for several years. The work required to he done was increasing, and it would isterease,thoogh very Slightly, but the expenses would not increase so rapidly as they would an in other departments of the Corpora- tion, such for instance as the Paving and Sewerage Committee. Their sales last year were larger than dur- ing the previous year, amounting to £3,457. That wes the value of the manure which was sold during the 12 months, being an increase over the preceding year,which was considered a good one, of £226. The quantity made last year was larger than ever before by 537 tone, and tney had £26 worth partially dried at the works which had not been taken into stock. In addition to making and selling a large quantity,t hey had kept up the quality of the manure, which was quite evident from the analy- sis of Mr. Stnetham. An item, in the expenditnre he Pointed out, was the constructien of two steel vans, which were being made, steel being a mote suitable material than wood. One of the minutes of the com- mittee was to the effect that the chairman. depety- chairman and Mr. Dees be appointed to attend the con- gress of the British:lnstitute of Public Health, to be held in London on the 26th • and 31st July. He had never been on a rt putation himself, but he believed that no amount of reading at the fireside could be as effective as coming into Contact with people at conferences—(hear, hear)—where they got informa- tion that was really worth having. Councillor BEAMAN seconded the motion. Councillor Hurcurtesote objected to the deputation and resolution, aithotigh he said he should not move an amendment. The same Principle was involved in this as sin the previous case. ' Alderman Scrercrei remarked that Councillor Hutchin- son's objections showed a little bit of jealousy in conse- quence of the question introduced eta previous meeting with regard to the painting of the steam fire engine. (Laughter.) Councillor HUTCHINSON objected to. such a. remark being made. Alderman SUTTON': Because the Council did not think it of sufficient importance that a deputation should go to London to see that little work done, it did not for a moment follow that an important deputation like this should hot go. (Hear, hear, and renewed laughter.) Councillor Motors in reply to certain criticisms on the estimates, said he was as anxious as anyone that the estimates should not be exceeded if it were possible to keep them down, and with that object iii view they were having prepared a monthly statement which. enabled them to check off month by month their actual expendi- ture, and to see whether an increase took place or not. With such a control it was not likely the expenses would be increased. (Hear, hear.) . The minutes were then adopted.

•PAYING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTRE. The estimate of the committee's expenditure was VAG 19s. fkl . Alderman WRIGHT, in moving the consrmation of the minutes of the committee, said that with regard to the highway department, it was not their intention in future to buy any horses. They would hire what ani- mals they required, as they considered it would pay thews better to clO so (" clnistion:") Although the borough was increasing so rapidiv,the committee during the bast year kept .£4O within their estimates. (Hear, bear.) Councillor BEATON seconded the motion. Councillnr.BENNwrr asked when it was proposed to proceed with the paving of 13.40 k-st. Alderman WRIGHT : As soon as we can spare the time and get the materials we shall go on with the work. The minut.s were agreed to. XVSUI. &C., COMMITTER.--.THE COUNTY COUNCIL AND

THEIR+ GRANTS. Councillor .ROBERTS, in moving the confirmation of the Inmates of the Committee, said he had mtv3it pleasure in expressine• on behalf of the Committal, their great satis- faction with the bust of the late Lord Wimnarleigh,betlt on account of the association of his lordship with War- rington. and because the bust was not only an admir- able likeness but an excellent work of art. (Hear, hear.) The-minute with reference to the Technical In- struction Committee was a most important one. " A letter from the Technical Instruction Committee of the Guilty Council stating that no further grantsscould be made in reeponWe to an applicaeon of this committee was teed." The County Council had refused to give a further grant out of the excessive income they had two veers ago. They received their ordinary grant of a ,little,ver £6OO, but they applied for a further grant, because of the excess of income over the expenditure. 'The County Council had £15,000 or:£16,000 to dispose of, 4itit of which the Museum Comtnittee thought they were entitled to some extra consideration, bemuse the -money was there for the purpose, and because they had not received that proportion of the County Council grant far technical instruetion to which they would have , been entitled if they had been a county borough, and whieh their population now entitled them to becomm. It was very hard lines indeed, seeing that they were the : largest non-county norough in 'Lancashire. • , The CHAIRMAN :In England. 'Councillor Roamers proceeding said that unless they I got more favourable consi&ration before long they would be ful'y jusdfied in asking the Council to take steps to constitute Warrington a-county borough. (FiNtr, hear.) Technical instruntien was 140 important to the trade and commerce of the country, and to the town, that they could not afford to have their hands tied: Some one else was getting the benefit (if the money to which they in Warrington were entitled.. Councillor GREENING seconded the motion, whicl was carried. Tows HALL, PARK AND MATES COMMITTEE. THE NEW GATES.

This Committee's estimate of expendi:tire was £3,193 Councillor Bovroxr moved the eonfirrnvion of the minutes of the committee, and allude.l tt-ethe stun of £5OO for alterations to offices and office furniture at the Town Hail. He said that that expenditure had neer thrust on the committee by the action ,of the Water Committee and the Gas Committee in reqoiring het,'.et facilities for the collection of money. Toes' enalci not say whether the work would be carried oiA•that year or not, but it was considered advisable to h ye the money in hand. Then there was an item of £5O for laying out the ground in front of the Town Hall. They mild not know whether the mosey would be requirod this year. There was also a sum of £5BO for gates, pallsading and fixing ditto,the estimates altogether being £3,193. There was no item they could curtail in any direction. Alderman WRIGHT seconded the passing of the minutes. - Councillor GREENING.—When may we expect the gates ? Councillor SMETHURST would like to ask whether the committee had thoroughly examined the Town Hall buildings? Could they not Znd accommodation for the few clerks who were wanted? There were only about two clerks in the water offices, and he contended that there was plenty of room in the building without spend- ing £5OO. There were half a dozes rooms which were empty. Councillor BOLTON, in answer to Councillor Greening said it was expected that six weeks would elapse before they received the gates. Being an engineer himself, Councillor Greening knew the difficulties which existed with regard to the gates. With reference to Ceuncillor Smethurst's observations, there were sevet al members of the committee who where of a similar opinion—that the Town Hall was quite large enough for the clerke,hut the clerks considered it was not large enough, arid they were continually grumbling about being" cooped in a corner." They expected when the stables were removed that very elaborate offices would be built, but as the item was only one of £5OO, the committee would do what they could do with it and no more. The clerks would have to be satisfied witb what they could get (Laughter.) The minutes were then passed. MARKETS COMMITTEE.—SUGGESTED IMPROVEMENT.

At a meeting of this committee the estimate of expen- diture was put down at £1.526. It was resolved that the resignation of Mr. Crabtree, the assistant inspector of weights and measures, be accepted, and that the vacancy be advertised. Alderman BLACKIIURST moved the confirmation of the minutes. Councillor HILL seconded. The CELLIRXAN said he was very glad to hear Alderman Blackhurst say they had a big income but did not spend much. It would be a good thing if the committee would spend some money and cover that porti‘en of the road over between the two markets leading from Heath Side to Peter-st. It was excessively cold for peop!e,and thi sds that werx brougied there were very necessary,

They were generally veeetables. Alderman BLACKHURST replied that the matter had been under the consideration of the • commit,ee, but they c')uld not see their way to carry out the work. They had an estimate of the et,at, which amounted to about £6OO, for which they would not get a penny in return.

The minutes were passed. RIVERS COMMITTEE.—THE SHIP CANAL. The estiMate of expenditure by this committee is £5O for fixing gauges. testing the flow of water, &c. It was resolved that the Surveyor Prepare a map showing, the position of the Ship Canal in relation to the borough, with the heights of all weirs between the Bollin and Bank Quay. Councillor Rosetrrs moved the confirmation of the minutes, and sad the only matter he need. refer to was the item of £5O, which arose in consequence of their having to watch the interests of Warrington in connec- tion with the Ship Canal; and the pOwers of the Canal Company; He did not wish to say more about the matter at that stage. ' Councillor Worms said they had not got any forwarder With respect to the negotiations about the lay-by, but the Ship Canal Company were pfrparing a crane at Latchford to deal with any tra.ffiz that might be going to or from Warrington. The minutes were then agreed to. FIRE ENGINE COMMITTBE.—THE WORKHOUSE WATER SUPPLY. . . The estimate ef expenditure is £482. It was resolved that the Guardians be recommended to lay on an eight- inch water main to the workhouse with proper and sufficient hydrants. Councillor HUTCHINSON moved the confirmation of the minutes, and remarked that the committee thought the supply of water at the workhouse would be insufficient in the event of a big fire breaking out. • ,COl.lllCiliOT SMETHURST seconded. The minutes were agreed to. . WATER COMMITTEE.

It was resolved that, upon the application of Mr. A. Lister-Kaye. the main in Manchester-road, be extended om Bruche House to Bruche Lodge,at the cost of £125, upon an undertaking being given to pay 01.0 per annum for five years (such sum to include a supply for doinegic purposes until the water rate yields that amount), and to pay the cost of laying the main to Bruche Hall and }Perm, the charge for water to be at the ordinav domes- tic rate. The minutes were confirmed, en the motion of the CHAIRMAN, seconded by Councillor Eleeneep, , FINANCE COMMITTEE.—THE RATES THE BOROUGH. The minutes of the committee, retain principally to financial matters, were of a lengthy character. The elewing is a summary of the esti metes :—Borough rate, £10,347; improvement rate, £25.18?; general sewers rate, £876; making a total of £36,381. The improve- ment rate aas fixed at 33. 83. in the £, and the general sewers rate at 21. in the L. Councillor Sleeve-Gems moved the confirmation of the minutes, and said he sincerely regretted the absence of Alderman Holmes. who for 30 years had had the duty of proposing the resolutions referring to the estimates. The estimaee of the Finance Committee for the coming year was £6,534, which was not in excess of last year's es,imate. Certainly last year's estimate was only £5,174, but salaries in the water ant gas departments were credited to the Finance Committee, and practically 1 their estimate did not exceed that of last year's. Pro- needing to the general estiinact, s of the, borough, he Was glad to noticethat there was suee an amount of interest being taken in the financial department this year. It arose undoubtedly from the fact that the rates were being enormously increased upon what they were two years ago. A rate of 6s. 6.1. in the L for a small bor- ough of less than 60,000 inhabitants could only be exces- sive, and it behoved everyone of them who had the care of the spending departments to de their utmost to keep down theexpenditure as much a-spossible for some time to eome. The expenditure of the year 1891-2 was •about the average expenditure of the borough, abid that was something like £30,000. Now they were expending £36,381, which was one-fifth in excess of what ought to be the normal expenditure ttci the town. The borough rate was the first portion to claim their attention in the general expenditure. They were asking the over- seers for a sum ot £10,347, being £BOO odd in excess of what they asked for last year. That arose entirely from the expenditure of one committee, the Town Hall, Park, and Baths Committee, who had asked for about £9OO in excess of the sum they asked for last year—£soo for stabling, and somewhat the same amount for the railing in front of the Town Hall. He did not blame them for that, as the Town Council had adopted their resolutions and they were only doing what they were entitled to do. With reference to the improvement rate, the item was considerably less than last year. But he must call their attention to the fact that they put back or postponed iesum of £2,700, The Committee had in their wisdom done this b.- lieving that they had a reasonable expecta- tion of that sum being relieved during the present year. Instead of that however the Health Committee had over spent their estimate by a sum of £l,BOO and the Sani- tary Works Department by a sum of £592. If they put these two sums with the sum which the Finance Com- mittee made over of £2,700 it would be discovered how it happened that they had to _ask ter such an increased sum this year. During the past year they had paid off £3,260 on capital charges of the borough, but unfortun- ately they did not stop there. It seemed to him that year after year.although they were paying off these large sums, they were still increasing their capital expendi- ture. After paying that £3,260 they were practically £5OO deeper in debt than they were this time last year. The rates last year amounted to £26,839 17a. 9d., and when he told them that the whole of that enormous sum had been collected with the exception of £2s,they would readily understand that they owed no small measure of praise to the officers of the Corporation who had done this duty so thorougnly and so well. (Hear, hear.) Councillor NETHERD seconded the confirmation of the minutes, and remarked thatthe 33. J. in the £ included sd. in the brought over from last year as pert of the expenditure in connettion with the smallpox epi- demic. Councillor BC2LTON said he did not know whether the allusion to the Town Hall, Park and Baths Committee having contributed to the high rate was intentional, but he should like to ask if the increase was net owing to the Finance Committee requiring money to be spent on the Town Hall to make more room for their lerks. (Hear, hear.) He thought the Chairman of the Finance Committee might have named that at the same time. They were not shown distinctly how the increase in the, rate was brought about, or how_ it was going to be re- duced. The Sanitary Committee was now broken up into three committees, Health, Sanitary Works, and Scavenging Department. In the year 1890, the esti- mate for this ennunittee was £9,992 ; in 1891, £10,381 ; 1892. £12,377; 1893, £14,401; 1894, £14,581, hch meant for the last two years alone an equivalent to Bd. in the £on the rates. It appeared as if there was going to be a long period of high rates, especially as they said it was impossible to work on Nes. Longford Depot had been a kind of sink-hole for the rates of the town, and it appeared likely to con- tinue so. If they were to reduce the rates they would leave to begin on a different system than they had been accustomed to. Councillor GREREINO thought the Finance Committee were r,ther to be congratulated on the statement ev..ich they had put before the Council. It was not their fault that there had been a smallpox epidemic in the town. That the capital expenditure was increasing was a good sign, because as the town increased the capital expendi- ture would increase. He Would ask the Chairman of the Finance Committee whether he had noticed the new Lorel Government Act for 1894, better known as the Parish Councils Act. Under that Act, the Council by making application to the Locil Government Board could take over the duties and powers of the overseers, sad they could collect their poor rate and improvement rate from one office, and with practically one stsff, and thereby reduce their expenditure considerably. (Hear, hear.) The Tows CLERK said it was quite true, as Councillor Greening had pointed out that the new Act gave power to the Corporation to apply to the Local Government Board to he entrusted with the power to appoint over- seers and assistant overseers, and which would give them the control to a great extent of the collection of the borough rate. The matter had been under the notice of the Finance Committee, and he (the Town Clerk) had received informal instructions to make the necessary application when the time arrived. He was preparing a report on the new Act, which did not affect the Corporation very materially. It made a few changes and conferred a few additional powers. The minutes were then agreed to.

div.head: CLERGYMAN SURPRISED. .
div.p: A CLERGYMAN SURPRISED. .
(From the " ltushden Times.")

A remarkable story has been related by Mr. James Mackness, a retired member of the Medical Staff Corps, w'ho had been in foreign service in India, Africa, Egypt, and Ashantee, and who, in the year 1892, was, after returning to his native place, ttricken down with paralysis. Thousands of the inhabitants of Rushden can vouch for the truth of the, narrative, and a representa- tive of the " Rushden Times" has elicited the following particulars : One Saturday night in the month of February, 1892, Meekness retired to rest, hale and hearty. As far as he knew he slept well through the night, but when he awoke on Sunday morning he lay a helpless mass of flesh and bone, and speechless. Previous to this cala- mitous affliction he had never suffered a day's seriou illness. For tw,s months he was unable to shift his little finger, much less the legs and arms which had . served him wAI during the forty-two years of his life. The sudden attack was the theme of conversation with the inhabitants, amongst whom Mackness was a favourite. Everything that could be done was done for him. The doctor was summoned, hut after prescribing a few bottles of medicine, could not give any hope of Mack- ness' recovery. The patient was removed from his bed in a cab to Northampton Infirmary, where he stayed as an in-patient four or five weeks; but when he came out he was very little better and this disappointment preyed so much upon his mind that he determined several times to commit suicide. He felt, he said, as though he hoped the earth would open and swallow him up. He told our representative it was impossible for him to accurately describe the depth of mental depression and physical latigour which he suffered. He lingered on at home in a dreadfully depressed and utterly hopeless condition. He could not have picked up a pin or a straw if anyone had cffered him 'ELMO. If he attempted to lift his arm above his head a strong retracting force held it down, and when extended horizontally, from the body the limb involuntarily wandered from the article it was intended to reach; in fact, all control over the muscular forces was entirely lost. It was in this sad condition that Mackness lay for fourteen months before he became aware of the life reviving properties of Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People, and he blesses the day he read in" The Weekly Budget" a cure of a similar affliction by the use of these wonderful restora- tives to health and strength. Mackness at once procured, through the kind services of a friend, a box of pills from the local chemist, and as they gave him immediate re- lief he took them until he was able to use his limbs and once more feel his feet and hands. Up to this time he had expended large sums of money in medicine electric belts, and electric batteries (the discarded electric belt was shown to the reporter), Mackness stating that the only good it did him was to keep his loins warm. After taking the pills, as directed, his limbs gradually resumed their natural elasticity, and his speech was retorted. The news of his recovery was regarded by his friends as nothing short of a miracle, and it became a subject of public conversation. The clergyman (Rev. Boyne-Bunt- ing); who met him out and about,expressed his astonish- ment at the remarkable change in the man whom he had visited when lying on the sickbed. .ee his recovery Mackness has been able to work, in the employment of Mr. Nattrass, ironmonger. Mackness attributes his mir- aculous recovery solely to the use of Dr. Williams' Pink Pills, as every thing else had failed to d* him good.

It is not alone in cases like the above that Dr. illiams' Pink Pills have a miraculous efficacy. They are recognised as one of the greatest modern medicines, a perfect blood builder and nerve restorer, and an un- failing cure for rheumatism, sciatica, neuralgia, partial paralysis, loeomotor ataxy, St. Vitus' dance, nervous headache, prostration, etc. Dr. Williams' Pink Pills restore pale and sallow complexions to the glow of health, and are a specific for all the troubles peculiar to the female sex, while in the cases of men they effect a radical cure in all cases arising from mental worry, overwork, or excesses of whatever nature. div.head: ST. PAUL'S CHURCH SALE OF WORK.
div.p: ST. PAUL'S CHURCH SALE OF WORK.

The annual sale of wcrk in connection with St. Paul's Church, Warrington, was held on Monday afternoon, in Heath Side Infants' schools. The sale was opened by M re. J. C. Parr, and there were also present :—Rev. H. V. and Mrs. Pigot, Rev. B. and sirs. Percival, Rev. J. C. Pigot. Rev. E. C. E. Carle- ton, Rev. Gibson Smith, Mr. Parr, jun., Mr. and Mrs. T. Morris, Mr. and Mrs. D. W. Finney, Mr. and Mrs. Robert Davies, Councillor and Mrs. Smethurst, Dr. White, Mr. and Mrs. D. Jones, Mrs. John White, Mr. and Miss Long, Mrs. Jeans, Mrs. Be.amont, Miss Smith, Mrs. Langham, Mr. A. Pigot. and Mr. H. G. Pigot. The Rev. H. V. PIGOT in introducing Mrs. Parr, said that the sale of work was a well-known institution in the St. Paul's parish, and most present were aware of the objects which depended upon the proceeds. Last year he gave them some idea of the great necessity they were under in promoting the sale of work. S.) many objects were dependent upon it that they must maintain the sum they obtained last year. Last year a grant ot £5O was made for Miss Westwell's salary, a grant of £5O to the curates' fund, £2O for the use of the clay school, £5 for the mothers' meeting, and £3 for the sewing class in connection with the Girls' Friendly Society, £2 for the banners and flowers for the church and Sunday school, besides £2O granted for the renewal of the church clock. If they did not realise a considerable sum, they would have to go short in some of these departinents. During the past two years they had had the Mayoress with them, and he had received a letter from her wishing the workers the best success. (Hear, hear.) Mrs. PARR said that she was very pleased to be able to help in any way the good work which Mr. Pigot was do- ing in the parish, and she had great pleasure in declar- ing the bazaar open. Councillor SrawrituesT proposed a vote of thanks to Mrs. Parr for her presence that afternoon. Mr. R. DAVIES seconded the motion. He heard a great many objections raised against sales of ovork, but he was very much in sympathy with them because they enabled them to meet together and see friends whom they could not always see, and they also promoted sociable- ness. Mr. T. AIORRIS supported the motion which was carried unanimously, after which the buying and sel- ling commenced. There were stalls in the room prettily arranged with useful and ornamenttl articles. There were also a refreshment stall and a flower stall. The following were the stall holders :—Mrs. Chorlev, Mrs. Edwin Woods,Mrs.Gibson,Mrs.Smith,Mrs.Peacocke,Miss White, Miss Geddes, Mrs. Hepherd, Mi‘s Lvthgoe, Miss Craik, Miss Gibson, Mrs. Finney. Miss FirMey, Mrs. T. Morrie,Miss Coubrough,Miss Burton,Mrs.Smet hurst,Mrs. James Richardson, Miss Smethurst, and Miss Reid. The refreshment stall was in charge of Miss Westwell, Miss Shawcross, Miss Braide, Miss E.Ward, and Miss Sewart, (Haydock) ; bran pie, Miss E. Pickton, and Miss Rath- bone; flower stall, Miss A.Smethurst., and Miss D.Reid. The sale was onlv open for one day, and the proceeds amounted to £165 17s. lid.

div.head: NARROW ESCAPE FROM DROWNING
div.p: NARROW ESCAPE FROM DROWNING
AT RUNCORN.

COURAGEOUS RESCUE OF TWO CHILDREN. Twf. children named William Edwin Hall and Harry Bennison, aged respectively ten and five years, and both residing with their parents in Alsert-st., Runcorn, had mast providential escapes from drowning on Saturday afternoon. The little boys were both playing at about four o'clock on the bank of the Bridgewater Canal, near Savage's Bridge when by some means they fell into the water. The elder boy rose to the surface near the bank but the younger one rose in the middle of the canal. The screams of a i woman attracted attention to the accident and a young man named Thomas Parkes, of 19, Sutton-st., Runcorn, driver for Mr. Thomas Jones, Canal-st., ran to the side of the water and plunged in to the rescue of the children. Raving safely landed the boy named Hall he swam out to Bennison whom he caught by the hair of the head just as he was sinking for the last time. The child was borne to the canal side where he was soon restored to consciousness and in the meantime Parkes jumped into a cart: and was driven home. Both children were per- fectly well on Monday and appeared none the worse for the accident. The young man Pdrkes is deserving of the highest praise for the plucky way in which he rescued the ehildren. A number of people had congregated on the bank at the time but no one volunteered to enter the. water until Parkes came forward; and it is very pro- bable that had he not been at hand that the children would have been drowned,

div.head: MUSIC FOR THE INMATES OF THE WORKHOUSE.
div.p: MUSIC FOR THE INMATES OF THE WORKHOUSE.

The House Committee reported that the Warrington Amateur Minstrels had offered to give an entertainment to the inmates of the workhouse,and they recommended that the offer he accepted and that the performance be given on Thursday evening. They also recommended that the tenders of Messrs.N.B. Percival and Co. ,for grDcery, Messrs. Fletcher and Lee for drapery, Mrs. Chesters for brushes, and Messrs. Roberts and Sons, for boots and slippers, he accepted.—Mr. S. DAVIES, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, said that the entertainment took place at seven o'clock and would continue until nine. He was sorry that they could ri•t give any refreshments to the minstrels. They had not the power to do that. They were all teetotalers, and he hoped some kind friend would come forward and give the money necessary for the refreshments as the minstrels would he very dry after two hours' singing.—Mr. HEicroN seconded the motion which was 7.arried.

Mr. W. HOUGHTON said that he would like to call at- tention to a small matter which was not gone into at the last meeting of the Schools Committee. He wished to know how a tradesman who contracted with the. Guardians came to charge 63. for a whitewash brush. Perhaps Mr. Mines would be able to give some eiplana- tion.—Mr. Mines said that they only required one whitewash brush a quarter, and the brush rilerred to was a remarkably good one. He took it to a tradesman to see whether a reasonable price had been charged for it, and that person had said that NI would not like to sell a similar brush under 6s. 6 I.—Mr. Shaw said that similar brushes were supplied to tradesmen at 723. per dozen.—Mr. Houghton expressed himself satisfied.

div.p: GIFT OF ORANGES
The Superintendent of Padgate Schools reported the gift of a large case of oranges to the schools from Mr.W. Houghton.
A NEGLIGENT TOWNSHIP.
The CLERK rep7r;:i-th-a-t'all the townships in the Union had paid their calls except Peniteth. INSURANCE OF PROPERTY. _ -

The CLERK read a letter from the Liverpool. Lon- don and Globe Insurance Co., with reference to the proposed insurance of the Workhouse. The Company stated that for the first policy, their minimum rate was is. 6d. per cent., which was as low as they could man- age. However, they would send their Surveyor to examine the House, and he would give his report.—The subject was referred back to the Committee. THE LATE REGISTRAR OF CROFT. The CLERK said that he had received a letter from the Registrar General in which it appeared that an applica- tion had been made to him for an allowance to the widow of Richard Turner, who had been for 35 years the registrar for Croft. The Registrar General had re- plied that the application was out of his power to grant, and that it depended upon the poor-law Guardians. He (the Clerk) was of opinion that the Guardians had no legal power to grant an allowance. They might have superannuated Richard Turner during his illness prior to his death. He would advise the Guardians to pass a resolution expressing regret that having no legal power to grant anything, they could not comply with the application.—A resolution to tl;is effect was passed unanimously.

ALL SAINTS' BEWSEY-ROAD. WARRINGTON.

The aanual vestry meeting was held on Monday even- ing, the Vicar, the Rev. H. V. Pigot, in the chair. The accounts showed a balance in hand of £2 7s. Iod. Mr. T. Warley, parishioner's warden, remarked that the offertories during the past year had been better than they had ever been since the church was opened. The Chairman nominated Mr. P. Sudlow as his warden, and Mr. Warley was re-elected people's warden. Mr. J. Butler and Mr. Hall were appointed sidesmen. Votes of thanks were passed to various benefactors to the mission during the year, namely, to the ladies' committee of the sale of work, which had granted £2O ; to the Rev. H. G. Smith, rector of Halewood, who had given an altar cloth that had been in use at Halewood ; to the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton for the gift of a font.& which had been in use at St. Mary's Church before the consecration of St. Luke's ;to Mrs. Thomas Morris for a donation to- wards the cost of the Sunday school I anner ; to Mrs. Chorley for bearing the cost if relacvering the brass upon the cross, vases and altir and alms desk. and .o the ladies of the Latchford Church Wolk-rs' Society for a grant of £2 towards the funds of the mis&on. A vote of thanks to the Chairman brought the meeting to a close.

div.head: CHRIST CHURCH, LATCFIFORD.
div.p: CHRIST CHURCH, LATCFIFORD.

The annual vestry meeting was hell in the schoolroom Latchford, on Saturday evening. Tim chair was occu- pied by the Vicar, the Rev. B. B. Prescott, and there were also present—Toe R-Y J. Prescott. and Messrs. .1. VVhite, John Fairclougii, J. Coxon, J. Low, Margett's Banks, R. Kirkham, W. Starkey, J. Le., T. Starkey, W. Knight, Longhottom an R. Gorton. Mr. Coxon stat-d that the receipts were £289 9.... 51. and the expenditure £312 14s. 81., leaving an adverse valance of 23 5.. 3,1. With regard to the choir fun I, there was now only an adverse balance 01 12s 7ol.—The accounts were passed.— The Vicar said that lie was exrremely thankful to Mr. Coxon f(r his past services, and he was glad to be able to say that he ha .1 promised o serve again during the ensuing year.—Mr. S. Reynolds was appointed parishoners warden f,r the ensuing year. Votes of thanks were passed to the retiring officers for their services during the year. At the conclusion of the meeting Mr. Gorton asked if the Parish ()minas Act would affect Latchford.—The Chair nan I cannot say.—Mr. White observed that Latchford would be divided into two wards. What thore would be for the Parish Council to do he could hardly say.—Mr. Gorton : I suppose they will use the schoolroom, Cannot this meeting make a charge ? Mr. Fairclough : The school managers will do that.— Mr. White remarked that the school managers would fix the rate, and if any Jbjecjon was raised by the Parish Council, the matter would he settled by the County Council or some other authority. ST. MARY'S CHURCd, SANKEY.

The annual vestry meeting of the above church was held in the Sankey Schools, on Thursday, after a formal opening in the church. There were present: Rev. E. S. Jackson (vicar), Messrs. W. Taylor and W. P. Skelton (churchwardens), and Messrs. J. Millington, R. Board- man, Cartwright, Mainley, Longsliasv, J. B. Aitkin, E. Foster, Woods and Woodward. Mr. W. P. Skelton in presenting the accounts for the past year, said that the balance brought forward from the previous year had been £77 2s. 10d. The total church collection had been £2ll us. 6d., which made a gross total of £289 45. 10d. as income for the year. This left a balance in hand of £53 is. He thought this was very satisfactory, as the wardens did not wish to have a large sum of money hcarded up, and they had spent it for the benefit of the parish. There was a very gratifying increase in the attendance at church, and from Easter last year to Easter this year there had been 21,595 persons whe had attended church in the morning, an average of 424, and in the afternoon, 24,050, an average of 472. The total number therefore who had attended during the year had been 45,645, being an hacrease upon any previous year of 8,880. (Applause.) The number of communicants had been 1,355, an increase of 336 upon any previous year. These numbers were independent of the worship- pers at Penketh.—The Vicar said that this was the four- teenth time he had presided at the vestry meetings at Sankey Church, and he had received during the whole of that time the greatest possible kindness from the parishioners. He rose now to propose a hearty vote of thanks to the retiring churchwardens for their services durieg the past year. 'they had been very attentive to their duties, although Mr. Skelton had passed through much trouele. Mr. Millington seconded the vote of thanks which was passed unanimeusly.—The Vicar then nominated Mr. J. B. Aitken as his warden for the ensuing year.—Mr. Longshaw proposed the re- election of Mr.W.P.Skelton as people's warden. Mr. Car- twright seconded the motion which was carried unani- mously.—Mr. Skelton expressed his appreciation of the honour they had conferred upon him by electing him for the third successive year.—On the motion of Mr. R Boadman, the following were chosen as sidesmen : Messrs. W. Taylor, J. Millington, Longshaw,Cartwright Duinbell, H. N. Fairclough, Nerman,H. Ireland,Mainley, James Woodward, Forster, and .1. Warburton.—Mr. Skelton proposed and the Vicar seconded that Messrs. Aitken and Dignun be appointed delegates to the dio- cesan and ruri-deaconal conferences. The motion was carried.—Mr- R. Boardman was re-elected sexton on the motion of Mr. Mainley seconded by Mr. Cartwright.— On the motion of the Vfcar seconded by Mr. W. P. Skelton, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the choir, organist, choirmaster, and various officials for their services during the past year. This concluded all Ipublic business.
