The attendance at the meetine's of this Society shows no signs of diminution, and at the meeting on Sunday there was again a large gathering. Mr. John Crosfield. J.P., occupied the chair. In the course of the usual five minutes address he said he toolt an interest in everything which tPnded to make Sunday a pleasant day for work- ing' people, and expressed hin-Felf strongly in favour of the opening of reading,-noms and museums on Sundays. Alluding to the opening of his gardens and the exhibi- tion of his flowers, he thought that all these things were of an elevating and refining nature. Mr. Crosfield also spoke of his recent sojriurn in SwitzPrland and of the beautiful scenery of that country. He remarked that if he had the power he should like to have taken every per- son in Warrington to see the lake of Geneva.—Mr.J.Clia n- dos Wilson of Manchester, delivered the address for the afternoon, and took occasion of the day being the Ist of April to make some exceedingly clever and instructive observatious upon " prevalent-fools." He also referred to gambling, intemperance, swearing, and the spirit of complaining and grumbling at one's lot. Mr. Scatter- good and Miss L. Wallington each contributed a solo.

div.head: COUNT TOLSTOI'S NEW BOOK.
div.p: COUNT TOLSTOI'S NEW BOOK.

There was a large attendance on Sunday evening, at Cairo-street Chapel, when the Rev. %V. H. Drummond took for the subject of his monthly "Talks with Work- ingmen" Count Tolstoi's new book, entitled " The Kingdom of God is within yot4 ; or, Christianity not as a mystical doctrine, but as a new life conception." The rev, gentleman gave .a brief outline of the career of Tolstoi, as a nobleman, soldier, novelist, as voluntarily living the life of a peasatt with the peasants on his estate, and as a writer on Christian ethics. Tolstoi adopted as his standard the Sermon on the Mount, and had more particularly insisted on the doctrine of non- resistance, and in his present work he returns to the charge, and enters a vigorous protest against the mili- tary systems of the nations of the earth. His previ tug works on the same subject had met with hostility both from Church and State. His theological critics had been experts in silently ignoring and evading the crucial question, while his secular critics had regarded Christ's teaching as the beautiful dream of an impractical reformer, quite unsuitable for modern civilization. After quoting from the book Tolstoi's appeal for indivi- dual action in carrying out the teaching of Christ in the direction of non-resistance—" Each one has but to begin to do his duty, each one has but to live according to the light that is within him' to bring about the immediate advent of the promisel kingdom of God, for which the heart of every man yearng." Mr. Drummond said they might not agree with all Tolstoi said,but it was a strong book, an earnest book, a book to compel thought. It was full of faith and vivid realization of Christianity as a real life for men to live. It recalled them to the most serious problem which the Christian democracy had to face. It lay behind all the questions which were agitat- ing, society, our labour difficulties, our economic difficul- ties, our problems of progress and poverty. Jr was the hideous contradiction which gave the lie ta our belief in human brotherhood and the common Fatherhood of God. —During the service the choir rendered very tastefully the anthem, "Sing a song of praise," Mr. J. M. Muir presiding with his usual ability at the organ.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

Mr. John Mclntyre presided over the usual fort- nightly meeting of the Guardians held on Tuesday at the Workhouse, Dut ton. There were also present the following gentlemen :—Messrs. Joseph Knowles (vice-chairman), H. E. Heywood, J. M. Williams, C. T. Whitley, T. Lewis, E. Aaron, T. Brandreth, J. Weir, S. Yarwood, T. Handley, Jones, the Rev. J. Hanby; Mr. John Ashton (clerk), and Mr. George Ahton (a,sistant clerk). THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT ACT, 1894. _

The Local Government Boar l, writing in reply to a letter sent by the Clerk with reference to the Local Government Act, 1894, stated that the Act did not con- tinue in office the present chairman or vice-chairman of the Guardians, and the Board considered that there should be an election to those positions at the first meeting after April 15th. The Act also did not continue in office any committee of the Guardians beyond the period for which it was appointed. As regarded the Assessment Committee it appeared to the Board that the one appointed in April last must be considered to have been appointed for a year only, and that consequently a new committee should be appointed at the first gather- ing after April 15th. The School Attendance Committee should also he appointed annually. As to the committee of a Rural Sanitary Authority the Board stated that where such an Authority elegated their powers to a e' minittee, under section 201 of the Public Health Act, 1875. the de,eatinn could only be for the current year of office. The Board therefore thought that any such committee must be considered as ceasing to exist on the 15 h April. As regarded Parochial Committees it peartd to the Board th it there was nothing to continue them in °lice beyond the period for which they were appointed.

PLIOPOSIM LICENSING OF PRIVATE CLUBS.

A copy of a oetiton was forwarded by the Edmonton Union to the 8.-ard which had reference to the subject of licensing clubs, and which had been adopted by the Edmonton Board. The Board pointed out that serious e vils arose from the clubs in which intoxicants were sold to members without any limit as to hours, and expressed the belief that the licensing of such clubs and the re,triction of hours for selling intoxicants, besides bringin7, in an appreciable revenue, would not only tend to reduce pauperism, but be a great benefit to the coin. munity at large. They therefore trusted that the Chan- cellor of the Exchequer in the forthcoming Budget would make provision for placing clubs under the saint' restrictions as to license for, and hours of sale of intoxi- cating liquors as in the case ot ordinary public houses. —lt was decided to support the petition.

The annual meeting of the Holy Trinity Church vestry was held on Tuesday evening in the vestry under the presidency of the Rev. Dr. William Pres- ton, D.D. There were also present :--Nleesrs. C. A. A great amount of good had been effected, and he had receivt I valuable as- sistance from the wardens of the church—Messrs. Tim• mini and Hankinson, who ha l worked indefatigably for the cause. div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAM EN P.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAM EN P.

MONDAY. In the House of Commons on Monday evening Mr. MIINDELLA, replying to a question put by Mr. Provand as to the loss of the ship Port Yarrock, said the case was receiving consideration, with a view to further proceed- ings if possible. He was taking advice as to the best means of securing the seawo:thiness of merchant vessels and the Government also intended that a thorough enquiry into the question of übdermanning should be made by a Committee formed of shipowners, seamen, and Board of Trade experts, and containing also mem- bers of the House from both sides. Mr. JOHN MORLEY informed Mr. T. W. Russell that he was ready at any moment to move the appointment of the Select Committee on the Irish Land Acts, and he was not without hope that he might so alter the form that bon. members opposite might assent to it without discussion. Sir W. Harcourt intimated that it was his present in- tention to introduce the Budget on the 16th April. Sir G. Trevelyan moved the appointment cf a Stand- ing Committee of all the Scotch members, with fifteen other members nominated by the Committee of Selection for the consideration of all bills relating exclusively to Scotland which might by order of the House be commit- ted to them—a proposal, which would he said, enable the House at a most important stage of each Scotch bill to get the real opinion of Scotland. Mr. BALFOUR moved an amendment declining to sanction any change until the House had had an opportunity of pronouncing on a general scheme which should extend like treatment to hills relating to each of the other portions of the United Kingdom. The debate was continued till midnight,and then adjourned to Thursday.
TUESDAY.

In the House of Commons on Tuesday evening, on the order for the second reading of the London County Council (Tower Bridge Southern Approach) Bill, Mr. A. Gibbs protested against the clause embodying the bet- terment principle. Mr. R. U. WEBSTER said the promo- ten of betterment wanted to force on London and Manchester for their own political ends that which would destroy a large amount of property and harass and injure the ratepayers. In supporting the bill Mr. Stuart said the London County Council had now got in this great fight the assistance of the Corporation of Manchester, who had introduced a bill containing the same principle of betterment. Sir J. Lubbock pointed out that the bill promoted by the Corporation of Man- chester contained identically the same clause and was " backed" by, among others, the leader of the Opposi- tion. The bill wa3 read a second time, as was also the Manchester Corporation Bill. On the motion of Mr. G. RUSSELL it was agreed that the Committee of Selection should appoint a Committee to whom should be committed all local bills by which it was proposed to create powers relating to police and sanitary regulations which deviated from the general law.

Mr. S. SMITR gave notice that that day four weeks he would move a resolution on the Currency Question. Mr. H. Gardner, in answer to a question, said he had come to the conclusion that the law was sufficient to prevent fraudulent misrepresentation as to origin in the case of meat. He suggested that producers should bring under the notice of the Board of Trade cases in which there was evidence to show that the Merchandise Marks Act had been infringed. Mr. DALZIEL moved a resolution declaring it desirable to establish a legislature in Sco'..land for dealing with purely Scottish affairs. Sir G. TREVELYAN said his vote would be given in favour of the resolution, and Mr. Balfour spoke warmly against it. On a division Mr. Dalziel's resolution was carried by 180 to 170. WEDNESDAY. In the House of Commons on Wednesday Mr. J. D. Palmer moved the second reading of the Old Age Provi- dent Pensions Bill. He said the till limited the pensions to persons of 65 years of age anti upwards who were in need of aid. There were to be three classes of pensions —l, to those who had never received poor-law relief ; 2, to those who had provided in some way for their old . age ; and 3, to those whose misfortunes rendered them deserving of aid, though they had not been able to pro- vide even partially for themselves. Mr. Bartley, in seconding the motion, said the amount of the pension was to vary from 3s. 6d, to 7s. per week. Mr. SHAW- LEFEVRI3 stNge.sced that the promoters of the bill should c,,oseni to th adjourament of the dabate till the House was in possession of the report of the Royal Commission, as he could not accept the tneasure,and he did not want the House to disagree with it. It the Royal Commission reported in favour of tl'e scheme in the present till the Government would give further time for its considera- tion. Mr. CIIASIMMLAIN, as a member of the Royal Commission, said it would be an advantage to that body

if some indication of the sentiment of the House were given on the present occasion. Without expressing any opinion on the details of the bill, he was stronzly in favour of its principle. But he had no doubt that the mover of the bill would consent to an adjournment if the Government would give a day for the tliscussioa of this question after the report of the Royal Commission had been received, without making it a condition what the report should be. Sir W. Harcourt assented to this. Dr. Hunter said when hon. members saw the report of the Royal Commission they would find that the discussion that day had only touched the fringe of the subject. He moved the adjournment of the debate. After some furtlpr discussion the motion for adjournment was carried by 205 to 138, and the debate was adj,)urned till Wednesday next. The Patent Agents Bill was read a second time and referred to a Select Committee. The Prevention of Cruelty to Children Bill was also, on the motion of Sir 11. WEBSTER, read a second time. Several bills were postponed in consequence of opposition, amongst them the Shops (Early Closing) Bill and Mr. Schwann's Tram- ways Bill.

div.head: THURSDAY.
div.p: THURSDAY.

In the House of Commons on Thursday evening the. second reading of the East London Water Bill was op- posed, on behalf of the London County Council, on the ground that they had not had time to fully consider the report of the Royal Commission on the London Water Supply, and that if this and certain other bills were passed they would be prejudiced in their negotiations with the water companies. Mr. Saaw-LRI-F.VRE said he had come to the conclusion that there was a good deal of force in the objections of the County Council. In the discussion which followed Mr. Goschen, Sir R. Webster, and Mr. Chamberlain supported the motion for the second leading, which, on a division, was carried by 226 to 227—rralority 1. Mr. Romirrsom, replying to Mr. SCRWANN, said that. a proposal had been made by the Admiralty that Man- chester and Birmingham should be made centres for the examination of students in the naval engineering de- partment.

Sir C. Russmit moved the second reading of the bill to give effect to the conclusions arrived at by the arbi- trators hi the Behring Sea Dispute. Mr. BALFOUR warmly applauded the action of the Government in this matter, and Sir R. WEnsTEh pointed to the successful issue of the arbitratien as" a monument of what could be done by fair argument towards the settlement of in- ternal ioniil disputes." The bill was read a second time.

The debate on the motion for the appointment of a Grand Committee for Scotch Bills was then resumed. No progress, however, was made, the Opposition professing dissatisfarlion that no reply had been given to the peethes which had been made against the motion of tar Government. Motions for adjournment were moved and d"feated. At length Mr. MORLEY said he would no longer oppose adjoornment, and the debate Was ad- journed.

div.p: Mr. ASQUITH made an admirable addition to the political rhe-
Mr. Asquith.

toric of the week at Hudders- field on Wednesday. The speech was mainly on labour questions and labour policy, and on such a subject no one has earned during the last two years a better title to speak than the Home Secre- tary of the present Government. But he alluded also to one or two other matters. Re paid afine tribute to his old chief, now in retirement, and he bantered Mr. LABOUCHERE on his attempt to form a " cave " against the new leader. That cave, said Mr. ASQUITH, had turned out to be a crumbl- ing and perishible habitation ; "it consisted of a single cell of most moderate dimensions, tenanted for the moment by a solitary Political hermit whose gregarious instincts would before very long be found to have got the better of his temporary passion for isolation." In fact, it may already be said that Mr. LABOUCEIERE has quitted his little hermitage, and even if still persuaded of the un- suitability of a Peer-Premier he is giving the policy of the Government the support which was to be expected of a representative of Northamp- ton. Speaking at Huddersfield, Mr. ASQCITH could scarcely avoid alluding to the divisions in the army of progress which had been the means of handing several constituencies over the Tories, one of those constituencies being Huddersfield itself. He made no attempt to apportion the blame for those divi- sions, but he very urgently advised re-union. And he very clearly put his finger on the cause of these intestine distractions. Amongst progressives there is a van-guard and a rear-guard, and at times the distance between these two parties becomes too great to allow of satisfactory co-opera- tion. While not pointedly advising either party, Mr. ASQUITH referred to the new forces that are appearing in politics and to the new ideals which are stimulating men's minds and imaginations. These forces and ideals can not be ignored if the Liberal party is to fight as one united phalanx , against that army of reaction which is always With us. Turning then to the labour questions which formed the staple of his speech, Mr. ASQUITH could point to a splendid and unique record of work lone and of still more work that had been attempted. He spoke with justifiable warmth of tho manner in which the working classes of the ' country had been deprived of the protection of the Employers' Liability Bill. That result had been , brought about by the combination of two great powers—the London and North-Western Railway directorate and the House of Lords. If, added Mr. ASQUITH, the millions of workmen in this country who are engaged in dangerous and hazard- ous industrial occupations allowed provisions for their safety to be set at nought by these two powers they deserved anything that befell, them. We believe, however, that he was right in his anticipa- tion that the workmen of the country, Conserva- tive and Liberal alike, will decline to accept this. rebuff. They will when the occasion and oppor- tunity arrive express their desire for the Bill in a fashion that will very ,effectually upset the cal- culations of privileged legislators and great rail- way directors. While admitting that all the legis- lative work of the Government had not been crowned with the result that was hoped for, the HOME SECRETARY claimed with pride that, in the matter of administration the Government had achieved more for the. workmen employed by it than any .other U-overnment had ever dreamed of. In all the great labour-employ- ng War office, the Admiralty, the Post Office and the Education Office—the condition of a vast number of workmen had been improved, by the shortening of hours, the raising of wages, or in some other way. In administra- tion the Government had not been fettered and frustrated by an obstructive Opposition and a Chamber of hereditary legislators, and in that sphere their labour policy has been enlightened and beneficent.
AT the meeting of the Manchester.

The Ship canal. City Council, on Wednesday, a nate of disquietude was struck with regard to the Ship Canal, or at all. events, there was an anxious desire evinced for further informa- tion. The Canal has now been open more than three months, and naturally many people, and especially those who are financially interested, as the ratepayers of Manchester are, would like to! know what the receipts have been during the three months, and what are the prospects, imme- diate or remote, of a dividend. Although the Manchester Corporation is well represented on the Board of Directors of the Canal,there aPpears to have been some impediments in the way of the presentment of a report to the City Council and through them to the ratepaSerm. At least that seems a natural inference from the language of Sir JOHN HARWOOD. This gentleman is the most influential and best known of the representatives of the Manchester Corporation on the Canal directorate, and he bluntly averred that if he had had his own way there would have been a report long since. There are few people in this part of the country who do not wish the Canal to be a complete success in every respect, financial and otherwise, and therefore it will be noticed with some apprehension th at there was a somewhat dubious tone about Sir Jouri HARWOOD'S remarks. He expressed a hope that a report would soon be presented by the representatives of the Corpora- tion which would be "satisfactory "—or, rather, as he at once amended his own way of putting it, that " would afford information to the Council." It is to be hoped that the information when it is reported will be satisfactory. No one, of course, ever expected that by the mere opening of the Canal the difficulties which are incident to so great an undertaking would be entirely overcome,

:7717,71 The Elections.
THE" miniature general election," as the group of bye-elections

fought this last week or two has been called, has turned out satisfactorily for the Government. In all but one of the seats the Liberals were on the defensive and the Tories had the opportunity of making a gain. But no seat has been lost, and in one or two instances the polling has been significant of progress. In Mid- Lanark the Liberal candidate has been returned by a substantial Majority over his Tory opponent in spite of the fact that a labour candidate drew away more than twelve hundred votes. It is to be hoped, however, that in this constituency, and in some others that could be named, successful attempts will be made by the progressive poli- ticians to settle their differences before another eleetion comes round. It is said that one result of the election has been to dampen the ardour of the Unionists for a general election. They have been loudly boasting that the" flowing tide" is with them, but since those elections have taken place they do not seem to be so sure that the tide is flowing in the right direction.

Mr. Daniel Bisbrown read a very intn-esting and in- Fc-ructive paper a,t, the weekly meeting of this class on Wedne,:dav evening, dealing with the " Catacombi of Rome." Mr. T. Simister cccupied the chair, and there was a fair attendance. A discussion ensu..(l in which Captain LeConteur, Messrs. John D. Jrnes, James Pali, ad T. Sinister t,-)ok part. FORTHCOMING ENTERTAINNENT AT ROW:MN.

It will be seen from an advertisement in our columns that a grand entertainment is to he given on April 19th in the Primitive Methodist New Schoolroom, Runcorn. Taloleaux vivants will be presented, also in- stances ot rapid sketching and instantaneous photo- graphy. The proceeds of the event will be is aid of clearing off the debt on Trinity Church and Ragged Mission.
LOCAL INVALIDS.
Sir Gilbert Greenall, who is staying at his son's residence at Tilstone, has been seriowly ill, hut has now taken a turn for the better. Mr. Joseph Davies, J.P., also continues to improve.
WARRINGTON HORTICULTURA.L SOCIETY.

The Warrington Iforticuitural and Floral Society have arranged to hold a show in the Gymnasium on August 22nd and 23rd : over three hundred prizes will be offered, and a large number of entries are anticipated.
FIRST WARRINGTON PEERS ECONOMIC BUILDING
SOCIETY.

Another ballot meeting of this Society was held at the Offices, 19 King-st., on Tuesday Evening. In the absence of the president, Mr. John Johnson was voted to the chair and was supported by several directors and a fair attendance of members. Messrs. Clegg, Newall and Williams were appointed scru- tineers to conduct the ballot proceedings which re,ulted in No. 106 being drawn, and this number being held by Mr. Edward Hardman, wire drawer, for four shares, he became entitled to the use of £4OO free of interest for 102-3rd years. The usual votes of thanks to the chairman and scrutineers con- cluded the business. LORD GEORGE SANGERS CIRCLTS. •

Next Friday the public of Warrington will have an opportunity of witnessing that celebi ated hippo- dramatic exhibition—in connection with Lord George Sangers' Circus—which has long been one of the sights of Llndoa. The performance will be given for the first. time out of London for almost half a century. Besides the various equestrian features of the circus, combined with the wonders of a menagerie, there will be spectacular perform- ances of the Soudan War. According to the adver- tised announcements hundreds of reserve men of the British army have hen engaged, a detachment of Arab soldiers and Red Cress nurses. One of the chief features of the circus is the wonderful clair- voyhnt and talking horse (grandson of the racing horse " Robert the Devil ") named "Tipster " which is remarkable for giving the names of winning horses in the seasons races. Further particulars,as to prices, &c., will be found in our advertising columns.

Orine's Quarry, Higher Runcorn, resulting in a lalwourer, named Peter 13 rber, 20, Shaw-street, Runcorn, sustaining injuries ti his body, legs and feet. It appears that the men at the quarry were resuming work after blasting operations had ceased, when a large stone became dislodged and fell, striking the man named, and badly cutting another young man about the head. div.head: FATAL ACCIDENT AT WIDNES

An inquest was held on Saturday, a the Widnes Accident Hospital, by Mr. S. Brighou3,e, on alp s),,iv of Peter Culle,n, Woodstreet, foreman labourer at Messrs. Pillingtox's works. On January 9, the deceased was working near some railway metals. It was•very foggy at the time and he was knocked down by a passing train and a wagon ran over his left foot. He was taken to the Accident Hospital and on examination it -wac found neceF,sar to amputate the injured limb. Drs. Hutchin- son m;3 pQrformed the operation. The deceased gradually- became weaker and died on Thursday the29th March. -A verdict of " accidental death " was returned.

div.head: WOUNDING CASH AT WIDNES
div.p: WOUNDING CASH AT WIDNES

On Tuesday at the Widnes Police Court, before Coun- cillor W. W. GnsFa,ae, a imiddle-aged woman named Elizabeth Bushell, of E lmund-at., was charged in cos- tidy with having assaulted A. woman named Margaret McCann, on Mondar. About two o'clock the prisoner went to prosecutrix's house and used had language. Both of them went inside the house and a struggle followed. ProFiecutrix was pulled to the floor by the hair of the head, and the prisoner bit off a portion of her left ear. Dr. O'keeffe proved attending the injured woman, who was suffering from a lacerated wound on the left ear, about two inches in depth, a portion of the ear had been entirely taken away. The prosecutrix was in-a danger- ous condition. On the application of the police the pri- soner was remanded in custody until Monday.

div.head: ALLEGED RAILWAY ROBBERIES NEAR WIDNES.
div.p: ALLEGED RAILWAY ROBBERIES NEAR WIDNES.

On Tuesday at the Widnes Police Court, before Coun- cillor W. W. Gossage, William Miller, Elephant-lane, Thatto Heath, St. Helens; Henry Gaskell, Lower Ince, near Wigan; and John Foster, 'Matto Heath, were charged with stealing 1191. yards of cloth, valued at ahout £3O, from the Rainhill Station,on the London and North Western Railway; and George Miller and .James Miller, both of Lower Ince, near Wigan, and Thomas Lowe, of Wigan, were charged with receiving the • cloth knowing it t have been stolen.—Mr. Preston and Mr. Bland prosecuted on behalf of the Rail- way Co., Mr. H. Riley, St. Helens, defended Foster, and Mr. W. Lees. Wigart,-defended Lowe. After a good d3al of evidence had been given the prisonors wore committed to take their trial at the County Quarter Sessions.

div.head: FATAL TRAP ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.
div.p: FATAL TRAP ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.

On Sum:lay afternoon, Mrs. Doyle, aged 64, licensee of the Crown Inn, Ann-st., waq out in a trip with Mrs. Jamieson, Mr:. E. Doyle, and a boy named William Jamieson. They were returning home and on nearing Farnworth the pony became restive. Just as they turned the corner of the road near the Horns Inn, Fara- worth, the pony took fright and the trap was overturned, throwing out all the occupants. Mrs. Doyle was thrown into a ditch a.nd had to be taken home, in a cab. She was attended by Dr. MacLennan, but gradually became worse and died on Monday night.—At the Widnes Police Court on Wednesday, Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquest on the deceased. The jury returned a verdict of Accidental death" and expressed their sym- pathy with the relatives of deceased, as also did the coroner.

div.head: MYSTERIOUS DEATH OF A WIDNES BOY,
div.p: MYSTERIOUS DEATH OF A WIDNES BOY,

A youth, named James Harper, aged 15, of 4, Lee-st., died under singular circumstances on Sunday evening. Deceased got home from his work about noon on Satur- day and seemed to be in good health. Shortly after he partook of a hearty meal, consisting of meat and pota- toes. La!er in the day he had a plain tea and for sup- per he again had meat and potatoes. Early on Sunday morning he awoke his parents,complaining of illness and vomited a great deal. He stayed in bed all Sunday and in the evening he became worse. The doctor was sent for hot death took place about 11 o'clock, before medi- cal aid could be procured.—On Wednesday morning,the inquest was held at the Adelphi Hotel, Lugsdale, before Mr. S. Brighouse, countg coroner.—Clara Harper, wife of James Harper, stated that the deceased was her son, and worked as a labourer at the Widnes Alkali Works. On Saturday he appeared quite well and before he re- tired to bed had a hearty supper of meat and potatoes. On Sunday morning, between one and two o'clock, h. complained of illness and vomited a great deal. He died ' about 11 o'clock.—Dr. Donald said he had made a post- mort?ln examination of the body. The stomach was distended, and there were signs of inflammation. In his opinion the cause of death was acute irritation of the stomach and intestines, probably brought on by error in diet. The jury returned a verdict in accordance with the medical testimony.

div.head: BAND OF HOPE ENTERTAINMENT AT RUNCORN.
div.p: BAND OF HOPE ENTERTAINMENT AT RUNCORN.

Under the presidency of Mrs. Meadowcroft a very enp-able entertainment took place on Wednesday in the Holy Trinity Church infant's schoolroom, Runcorn. The lady .delivered a brief address, after which a pro- gramme of songs, duets, recitation, dialogues, &c.. Wag admirably sustained by the male and female members of the Band of Hope. A cantata entitled "The Wan- dering Gypsies" was also contributed.

div.head: SRABESPERIAN RECITAL AT RUNCORN.
div.p: SRABESPERIAN RECITAL AT RUNCORN.

On Thursday evening an entertainment was given in the Runcorn Parish Church Sunday schools, on behalf of the prize fund of the National Sunday school. There was a large audience and the chair was talv.n by the Vicar who opened the proceedings with a brief ad-dress explaining the object of the entertainment. The pro- gramme included several recitals by Mrs. Wills Harper, well lrn own as a reciter, as well as various songs and duets by persons connected with the church. Mr. rtirkett Musgrove ably accompanied on the pianoforte.

AMUSING LECTURE ON " TEMPERAMENT" AT RUNCORN. At the weckly meeting of the Bethesda Literary and Social Class, Runcorn, on Tuesday evening, the Rev. R. G. Hughes, of Widnes, delivered an extremely interest- ing and amusing lecture on " Temperament." The rev. gentleman dealt with four chief classes of tamperament, namely, melancholic, choleric, sanguine, and phlegmatic and described each with its uses and abuses. The differ- ences between the sexes were touched upon, and the faults and virtues of each were frankly revealed, and received the censure or praise which they deserved.

ANOTHER CYCLIST CLUB FORMED IN RUNCORN. A meeting of cyclists was held on Wednesday evening in a room adjoining Mr. Riley's Cafe, Bridge-street, Runcorn, Mr. Clifford Le Couteur presiding. It was resolved that a club be formed and that the following gentlemen constitute a committee :—Messrs. Mack, C. La Couteur, Whinyate, Bockley, Wghington, Wright and Abrams. Mr. R. ,Moore, Church•street, was appointed hon. secretary', and Mr. J. H. Taylor hon. treasurer. Mr. Le Couteur was chosen captain of the -iaturday riders, with Mr. Buckley as sub-captain. Mr. Whinyate was selected captain for the Wednesday runs and Mr. Mack sub-captain. The meeting unanimously decided to ask Mr. S. Taylor to become the president of the club and also that the annual subscription ot mem- bers be 24. ,6d. The first run will take place on Satur- day, when a start will be made at 2.30, from Devonshire Square for Northwich.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. SAMUEL DOBSON, OF RUNCORN.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. SAMUEL DOBSON, OF RUNCORN.

We regret to record the somewhat sudden death of Mr. Samuel Dobson, aged 67 years, corn merchant, of 15 Bridge-st., Runcorn. On Monday evening about four o'clock he entered his house a:nd complained of a pain in his head and subsequently of another in his chest. He was falling but was caught by his wife who sent atones for Dr. Robinson. This gentleman obeyed the summons, but his attention and skill were unavailing and at 8.30 the same evening Mr. Dobson diedi apoplexy being the cause. The deceased was a nati4e of Runcorn and was engaged in his youth at the Runcorn Soapery, which employment he subsequently left for that of a baker in the establishment of Mr. David Williams, Itwell-lane. When nearly forty years of age he commenced busi,2.ess as a corn merchant on his own account, and success has attended him more or less since. He was of the Presby- terian persuasion and was for many years a Sunday school teacher, as well as interesting himself in the erec- tion of the new church and school towards which he has given handsome donations. He was also a staunch sup- porter .of the Liberal cause in politics and was well known amongst the most prominent Liberals in the town. The funeral took place in the Runcorn Cemetery yesterday (Friday) afternoon. -

div.head: FIRE AT A RUNCORN CLO TYING ESTABLISHMENT,
div.p: FIRE AT A RUNCORN CLO TYING ESTABLISHMENT,

- At about seven o'clock on Tuesday evening a tire broke out on the premises of Messrs. Unsworth, Bros., out- fitters, ot High-st., Runcorn, • and resulted in several pounds worth of damage being done to the stook. It appears that at the hour mentioned the gas in the win- dow of the hosiery and outfitting department was being lighted when a tie caught fire and spread to the other things which surrounded it. In the course of a few moments almost the whole of the stock in the window was ablaze and had it not been. for the praiseworthy conduct or-Mr. Sherratt, manager of the department, who speedily began to pull the things from the window at the expense of burning his hands somewhat severely, the result might have been much more serious. As it was, however, the flames were subdue by the aid of outsiders after the lapse of ten or fifteen minutes. A large number of shirts, ties, braces, collars, Br.c., were destroyed, but the property is fortunately covered by insurance. Messrs. .Unsworth wished to thank those persons who assisted the employes; in extinguishing the fire.

div.head: ALLEGED THEFT FROM THE PERSON AT RUNCORN.
div.p: ALLEGED THEFT FROM THE PERSON AT RUNCORN.

On Wednesday morning a woman named Winifred Casey was charged before Messrs. F. J. Norman and S. Taylor at the Runcorn Police Court,with stealing 9s.from the person of Robert Williams, captain of the schooner. " Alnwick ".on the night of the 3rd inst. The evidence adduced showed that prosecutor met with the woman, and want with her to a public house in High-street, where they had a drink together, Williams changed a sovereign in the public house, and put the change is his left hand trousers pocket. A man was with him at the time. Subsequently he accompanied the woman down towards the docks, but was turned back by the canal constable. They went hack into the town towards the railway station and after he had separated from her he missed the sum of 9s. from his trousers pocket. The woman was apprehended by P.S.Lee, but on being ques- tioned said the money had been given to her by the man Williams. The 93. was found by the officer secreted in the woman's left boot.—The prisoner on being ques- tioned by the magistrates repeated that the prosecutor had given her the 9s. She had been got into trouble by a young man some time ago. A lady in Higher Runcorn had promised to send her to a home, and she (prisoner) had made up her mind to go to the institution. If the Bench would allow her to go she promised never to come before them again, a:A would leave the town that day. —Ultimately the magisti-ateq--discharvd her saving that they seere in doubt as to whether the money had been given to her or not. They would give her the t'enefit of the doubt On condition that she left the town that day and never returned. Toe prisoner was then dis- charged.

A NOTABLE STUD OR HORSES. considerable amnunt of interest waA aroused among the agriculturalists and others visiting the Warrington Corn market on Wednesday, by a show of the valuable stud owned by Mr. S. B. Chadwick; of Crofton Lodge, Higher Roncorn,and Sutton Bridge Farm,Fro.isham. The animals were paraded about Horsemarket-street before the gaze of some hundreds of people, and admiration for the magni- ficent looking animals was freely expressed. Some- time ago'lllr. Chadwick parted with a very valuable stud and this was taken as an indication of his de- termination to retire from the prominent position as a stock breeder which he, has Dccapied for many years. However, the impression thus created was erroneous for Mr. Chadwick shortly afterwards re- emphasised his interest for practical desire to im- prove the stamp of horses in Cheshire, by collecting a yet more valuable stud.

div.head: CONSERVATISM AT WINWICK.
div.p: CONSERVATISM AT WINWICK.

The annual meeting Conservatives of the Winwick polling district (which comprises the townships of Southworth-with-Croft, Houghton, Middleton and Arbury, and Winwick-with-Hulme) of the Newton Division Conservative Association was held in the schoolroom, Winwick, on Monday evening, for the purpose of enrolling new members, electing a committee, officers. and representatives to the council for the ensuing year. There was a small attendance. Mr. Reginald Owen, son., of Croft, vice-chairman of the district, presided in the absence of Mr. George Comber, who had sent a letter of apology for non-attendance. Mr. G. Com- ber, J.P., was re-elected chairman : Mr. R. Owen, sen., vice-chairman ; Mr.E.O. Cooper, bon, secretary and treasurer for the disirict for the ensuing year. Messrs. Joseph Swinton, of Arlaury, and Samuel Thotnason, of Croft, were re-elected delegates to the council, the chairmen, vice-chairman, and secretary, being ex-officio members. The committee were re-elected, with power to add to their num- ber.

div.head: RUNCORN COMAIISSIONERS AND THEIR CLERK. --- ADDITIONAL SALARY.
div.p: THE RUNCORN COMAIISSIONERS AND THEIR CLERK. --- ADDITIONAL SALARY.

On Tuesday evening a special meeting of the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners was held at the Town Hall, Runcorn, for the purpose of receiv- ing a report from the Financial Committee as to the remuneration of the law clerk, and to pass such resolution as might be deemed-advisable. Mr. S. Taylor occupied the chair and the other members present were Messrs. F. Wiswall, W. Fisher, W. Collier, W. Bankin- son, J. Meadowcroft, T. Lea, W. fla.ndley, E. Itnison, D. Biebreven, P. Speakinan,J.P. C.C., and J. W. Lightburn. —Mr. Lightburn moved that the Board resolve itself into a committee in order that they could discuss the matter with greater freedom. The motion was carried and the Beard consequently went into committee. The question was then discussed and about an hour sub- sequently the meeting was again declared public. —Mr. Lightburn proposed that the recommendation of the Finance Committee be adopted.—The report showed that a letter from the law clerk was received at the meeting of the Finance Committee on March 6th and the consideration of the appEca.tion was adjourned to a special meeting on March 12th and again to the 19th,the law clerk being interviewed as to his duties, and the amount of income indirectly received by him in connec- tion with his position as law clerk to the Board of Commissioners. (1) The Committee unanimously and emphatically express their appreciation of Mr. Lake's, ability and to the assiduity with which he discharges all his duties. (2) The increased generll work of the law clerk since his appointment arising from the more vigor- ous action of the various committees and the, additional number of meetings he attends, is known to all the members of the Board, but perhaps it may be well to state that the Chairman of the Committee has examined the solicitors' letter books and found that while for three years ending 15th March, 1889, ' prior -to Mr. Lake's ap- pointment the correspondence occupied 52 pages of tne book ; for the three years ending May 1892, Mr. Lake's correspondence occupied 301 pages. Since this time the correspondence • has steadily increased. (3). As ex- amples of additional work the Committee may mention duties in connection with the newly acquired water works loans, street making and Technical institute. (4). The extra receipts for contracts and police court work paid for by outstanders does n )t. average £5 per year, notwithstanding the considerable time such work en- tails. The contracts and conveyances prepared from May last to date on behalf of the Board, and for which no payment is made to the law clerk would represent if paid for by ordinary client over £5O. They included town improvements, Technical Institute and mortgages and various amounts. The law clerk having throue.h his clients obtained loans' of over £3,000, has saved the town considerable sums for prosecution and solicitors' fees ; these during the past year at 11 per cent repre- sent £53. The course adopted by him as to Norman- road means the ultimate saving to the town of probably £2,000 and a present gain of great improvement and a contribution from owners of the Railway Company, namely, 15s. per head for owners of £ll5 for the Railway Company. The Committee have had conclusive proof of the duties and the serious manner in which the Board's work interferes with the private practice of Mr. Lake. (6) In view of the increased work and reeponsibility incurred by the acquisition of the Water Works, &e., and the future and immediate increase of work in preparing for and putting in operation the new Local Government Act, as well as the before recited increase of ordinary work, and in view of the law clerk's intim- ation that he would have to consider whether it was worth his while to continue hia duties at the present low amount of his eatery, as com- pared with similar officials, the committee reports and uneninseusly recommends that the law Clerk's salary be increased to £2OO per annum, such increase to coin- mencei the first Thursday in April, 1894, and that the major part of the increase be allacated to the water department, but that the exact amount of such allocation be left over until the end of September next, which arrangement it is anticipated will not entail any increase in the ratese—Mr. Speakman seconded the proposition. —An amendment was brought forward by Mr. Walter Collier to the effect that the matter be deerred until the Parish Councils Bill came into operation. It was pointed out that sines the appointment of Ma Lake his salary had been advanced from £llO to £135 per annum. the Board should also remember that Mr. Lake did not devote the whole of his time to the work, which was a fact that should weigh with the Board in coming to a decision. Mr. Imison supported the original motion.—Mr. Lightburn said that the proposal of the financial, committee was a matter of justice.— The amendment was defeated by seven to three and the original motion was subsequently carried.—Mr. Lake thanked the commissioners for their action in the matter and said he hoped to prove himself worthy of their con- fidence in the future as in the past.—This terminated the proceedings.

div.head: HALTON.
div.p: HALTON.

LOCAL SIICCESS.—We have pleasure in stating tha t amongst the successful competitors for County Council scholarships in physic° and chemistry is Mr. Jeacock, of Halton. The scholarship will entitle him to study these suljects at Owens College, Manchester. -

div.head: WESTON.
div.p: WESTON.

FARM FIRE.—On Thursday afternoon of last week, a hay stack belonging to Mr. James Ford, of Weston, was discovered in flames. The cause of the outbreak is unknown, but it is suspected that it originated by a child playing near the stack with matches. There was no necessity 'for the brigade as, the flames were success- fully subdued by the inhabitants of the district. The damage amounts to £25, but is covered by insurance. INTERESTING MARRIAGE.—At ,the Runcorn Parish Church on Tuesday, a very interesting wedding was witnessed by a large congregation the contracting parties being Mr. Thomas Ford, jun*.,of Cavendish Farm, Weston, and Miss Elizabeth Green, only daughter of Mrs. Green, of the Royal Oak Hotel, Weston. The clergy who officiated were the Revs. A. J. Jameson, M.A., and W. H. Stables, B.A. The bride, who was attended by five bridesmaids, was given away by Mr. Collier; whilst Mr. Percy Ford acted as. best man to the bridegroom. The ceremony being over the party returned to Caven- dish Farm where an excellent breakfast vraspartaken of. Later in the day the newly wedded pair journEyed by train to North Wales where it is intended to spend the honeymoon. A long list of useful and costly presents have been received. SUDDEN DEATH OF A WOMAN : THE INQUEST.—Mr.J. E. Worsley, coroner, :conducted an inquiry on Tuesday morning at the Proipect Inn, Weston. relative to tho sudden. demise of a woman named Alice Jane Summer- field, aged 33 years, late of 8, Heath-road, Weston. The testimony of the husband showed that he had only seen his wife once since September last, as he was passing the house of her mother. On the morning that she left him he found her under incriminating circumstances with William Tindsley, at witness's house. He ordered both of them out of the house. She admitted having misconducted herself, but he had never been divorced from her.—William Tindsley deposed to living with the deceased at Heath-road. On Friday evening at ten o'clock be retired to bed and she followed him in about half-an-hour. Both of them went to sleep, but at 3-30 the next morning witness was awakened ,when he found her dead at his side.—Dr. McDougall explained the result of the post mortem examination he had made. There were no external marks of violence on the body. The lungs were conjested and in his opinion the w,man had died from syncope or failure of the heart's action. —The jury recorded a verdict in accordance with the tnedia;.,deviflence.

HIGHWAY COMMITTEE.

This Committee recommended that an additional lamp be fixed at South Bank Terrace; that the penalties to which Mr. John Sefton and Mr. F. T. Bennie are liable under their contraets dated respectively 3rd and eth November, 1893, be remitted on the ground that this Board has not been able to keep them supplied with materials on account of the severe weather prevailing during the winter ; and that the time in each ease for the completion of the contracts be extended to April 30th, 1894 ; that the sum of Ell si. be paid to the Trustees of the Congregational Manse for a strip of land required for the widening of the Greenway-road end of Norman-road. That notices be pot up in Greenwav-road declaring the roadway over the Railway Bridge Greenway-road and the approaches thereto to be a highway and repairable by the inhabitants at large ; also that a copy of the above resolution and the Surveyor's Certificate be sent to the L. & N.W. Railway Co. On the proposition of Mr. Wiswall, 'seconded by Mr. Hankinson, the minutes were adopted.

div.head: HEALTH COMMITTEE.
div.p: HEALTH COMMITTEE.

This Committee reported that James Curzon was removed from Wivern Place to the Hospital suffering from typhoid fever, and as he was without medical attendance and was unable to obtain it, and as the re- lieving Officer had refused to give him a medical order, it was recommended that the action of the convnittee in providing medical attendance for such person be approved, and that the Local Government Board be re- questeclito sanction the expenditure thus incurred. Mr. Imison in proposing the confirmation of the minutes said the case was only a revival of the old difficulty which the Health Committee had had to face for a long period. The man was reported by a medical gentleman to be suffering from the infectious disease in que.ttion, and he expressed his determination not to attend the patient when he removed to the hospital. Thus they were told that if the man was sent to the institution there would be no one to attend him. After some dis- cussion the minutes were adopted.—On the motion of Mr. Handley it was resolved that the statement of the case be forwarded to the Local Government Board.

div.head: WATER COMMITTEE.
div.p: THE WATER COMMITTEE.

Among the reclmmendations of this committee were : that the tender of Messrs. Simp:son, Davies and Sons, for 1200 tons of slack at Ss. 10d. per ton, less 2 per cent discount, be accepted. The minutes were adopted. FINANCE COMMITTEE .

The monthly statement of this committee showed that the following amounts had been received on account of the general fund:—General District Rats £1266.135. 31., Market Rents and Tolls -.232 0,. 84., Slaughter Houses, .&c. .-210 12s. 11d., Night'Soil S.,les £8 153. Od., Cheshire Cowitv Council £62 10s. 0 Overseers of the Poor ' £l7 103. Od., Transfers £268 183. Od., making a total 01 £1668 193. 10c1. The other receipts were : Water Account, Rates, &c. £591 18s. 81. ; Water sinking fund transfer from water Riad £177, Private Street Works, Rev. Robert Fisher -.21503, District Fond, Sundries £3 145., Library Fund, Sundries £l3 ss. 84., Sinking fund, transfer £4-0, Technical Instruction account, Chesnire County Council £B5. The Committec also gave an estimate of the proposed expenditure for the year 1894-5 and showed that to meet them they would require a rate of 2s. lOci. in the £. They accordinglv recommended that a rate in two instalments of ls. 51. each in the £ be laid. The minutes were adopted.

div.head: F RODS HAM.
div.p: F RODS HAM.

MEETING OF THE PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE.—The fort- nightly meeting of the Frodsharn Parochial Committee was held on Friday (last week) under the chairmanship of Mr. A. Thomas, J.P.—Plans from Messrs. Linaker and Sons, Frodsharn, of proposed alterations to a house at Overton, were submitted ; also for the erection of a cottage at Netherton for Dr: Steele; and for four houses in Bridge-lane, Frodsha.m, for Mr. McWaters. These plans met with the approval of the Committee.—lt was reported by Mr. S. Davies that the water scheme was pro:rressing. Messrs. Timmins were • granted £350 on account of the contract. This was all the business of public interest.

div.head: 4* – THE ALDEMANIC VACANCY.
div.p: 4* - THE ALDEMANIC VACANCY.

A meeting was held in connection with the Liberal Council on Tuesday evening,for the purpose of considering the nomination of a successor in Council to Alderman Platt, it was decided,providing the Conservative party would agree,to offer the seat to Mr. F. Monks, C.C., J. P., as a recognition of the useful work he has performed—and is still doing— for the town. In the event ot the Conservative Party not accepting this proposal, it was decided to nominate a Liberal Councillor,
At a meeting last night of the Conservatives, the proposal from the Liberal Party was rejected and Councillor Hutchinson was nominated as the Conservative candidate for the seat.

div.head: WARRINGTON RURAL SANITARY.
div.p: WARRINGTON RURAL SANITARY.
AUTHORITY.

The monthly meeting of this Authority was held at the Workhouse. yesterday, when their were pre- sent:—The Rev. G. F. Roberts (in the chair),Messrs. lleaton, A. Jolley, Smith, W. Houghlon, S. Sutton (clerk), W. Owen (surveyor), Kerfoot (inspector), and Di. Sepliton_(medical officer).

SCARCITY OF WATER AT PADGATE. The Clerk read a letter from Mr. William Bennett. of Padga.te, and one from the Cheshire Lines Committee urgently requesting that a better water supply should he provided for Padgate. It was resolved that the Committee to instructed to enquire into the matter, and report to the Authority at their next meet- ing. SINGULAR APPLICATION FROM PENICETIL. The Clerk (Mr. S. Sutton) said he was in receipt of a rather singular application from the assistant oversee r Penketh (Mr. Jonas Foster) on behalf of a meeting recently held in Penketh. It wos to the effect that the Warrington Rural Sanitary Authority be approached with a view of having the cost of the street lighting reduced, and if this cannot be done, to discontinue the use of lamps. After some discussion it was agreed to Jake no action in the matter. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT._ - .

„ In his monthly report Dr. Sephton stated that there had been 33 births and 23 deaths, the excess of births over deaths. being then 10. The death-rate fro:n all causes was equal to 19-1 per one thousand, against 12 6 the average of the last three months, and against 8.9 in the corresponding month of last vea.r.—The report was adopted.—At the conclusion of the meeting a vote of thanks was passed to the Chairman, the Rev. G. F. Roberts, for his vrvices during the past year.

div.head: UNITED EVANGELISTIC MISSION AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: UNITED EVANGELISTIC MISSION AT WARRINGTON.

On Saturday night and during this week a series of united evangelistic services, promlted by the evangelical free churches of the town, have been held. The evangelists are the Revs. W. Y. Fuller- ton, and J. Manton Smith, and the meetings held have been, without exception, of a most successful character. The mission was commenced on Satur- day evening by a song service held in Bold-street Wes- leyan Church, conducted by the Rev. J. Manton Smith. There was a large attendance, and the rev, gentleman, besides delivering an impressive address, sang a solo,and considerably enhanced the musical portion of the service by playing his silver cornet. Mr. Smith also conducted four services on Sunday. In the morning at Legh-st. Primitive Chapel, and in the afternoon at Bold-street, a united Sunday scholars service was held. There were about 2,000 scholars present from various Sunday schools in the town, when Mr. Smith gave a most interesting address to the children. At the close he asked those under fourteen to write papers on the address he had delivered. Over fifty have been sent him during the week and some prizes are to be distri- buted this (Saturday) afternoon to the writers of the best papers. Two services were also held in the evening in Bold-st. Wesleyan Church. On Monday. Mr. Smith was joined by his brother missioner, the Rev. W. Y. Fullerton, when a mission service was held in Wycliffe Church in the evening, at which both evangelists took part. Besides the mission services which have been held ca('h evening during- the week, with the exception Of last night, three bible lessons were given on Tuesday, ‘Ved- ! nesday and Thursday afternoons. This Saturday after- noon) there will be anotivr young people's service at Bold-st. Wesleyan Church, and at 7.30 a song service will be given in Wycliffe Church. To-morrow (Sunday) morning the Rey. W. Y. Fullerton will prear..,h at the Baptist Church. Golborne-st., and the Rev. J. :VI. Smith will be at the Baptist Church, Latchford. A service for women will be held at 2.30 in Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church, and the farewell meeting will be at Wycliffe Church in the evening when both evangelists will take part.

Mr. Fred Brocklehurst,generll gecretary and organiser of the Labour Church movement, has been seleated as the Independent Labour candidate to contest Bolton at the next Priatnentary election, and has consented to to stand.

div.head: TOWN COUICIL Norm.
div.p: TOWN COUICIL Norm.

Finance was much in evidence at the meeting of Warrington Town Council on Tuesday evening. All the spending Committees—and most of the Com- mittees do something in the spending line—had prepared their estimates of expenditure for the next twelve months and these were submitted to the Council, and of course each chairman of committee had to go in some detail into the figures and to demonstrate how guiltless his particular committee was of anything in the shape of extravagance. This was done apparently to the mutual sati*faction of the various chairmen, and the awkward fact that the rates have reached the high point they now stand at was comfortably "negotiated." But, to begin at the beginning, the first business of the Council, was to hear read the letter in which Alder- man Platt resigned his aldermancy. The Deputy- Mayor (Alderman Francomb), who still presides in the absence of the Mayor, paid a tribute to the use ful services of Mr. Platt, and this tribute was added to by Alderman Sutton and Councillor Roberts. It was then announced that a special meeting will be held next Tuesday for the election of Alderman Platt's successor.

The Health Committee's minutes gave occasion for a slightly animated debate. Alderman Sutton pointed out that the Committee's estimates were lower than the estimates of last year by about £320, and taking into account the £l,BOO spent upon the small-pox over and above the estimates, the decrease would really be over £2,000. Council- lor Muir seemed to have misunderstood the drift of these remarks for lie demanded to know what were the exceptional causes which were leading to an increase of the estimates for the year, and he told the Committee that they " must really curtail expenses." Councillor Longton criticised the pro- posal to send a deputation consisting of the chair- man, deputy-chairman. and Mr. Deas to the Con- gress of the British Institute of Public Health to re held in London. He suggested that if the Com- mittee really desired the additional information that was to be had at the Conference they might diligently peruse the reports by their own firesides. On the other hand, Councillor Bennett was rather in favour of the deputation. He seemed to think that there was room for improvement in the man- agement of the sanitary affairs of the town by the Committee, and if they could get additional infor- mation by attending the Congress it might be a cheap bargain. Councillor Flood strongly resented the remarks of both Councillors Longton and Ben- nett. Their speec!es were, he said, the talk of street corners and grandmotherly gossip. But opinions differ, and Councillor Roberts affirmed that both the manner and method of the references to the Committee were perfectly satisfactory and perfectly proper. At the same time he maintained that the committee managed its affairs in an economical fashion, though in the face of the small- pox money had to be spent freely. Councillor Hutchinson spoke disparagingly of the proposed deputation,and moved that the part of the minutes relating to it should not be confirme I. This amend- ment was seconded by Councillor Hill. Councillor Plumpton expressed a desire for further informa- tion as to the proposed extension of the hospital, and he strongly urged that any further hospital ac- commodation should be provided out of the town, , where there was less population. In his reply, Alderman Sutton disclaimed any title to the mantle of a prophet, and dismissed a suggestion that had been made in the course of the debate that he should pledge the Committee to not again exceed its estimates with the remark that he had no con- trol over the smallpox or other possible epidemics. It these unwelcome visitants did not obtrude them- selves—well he thought. the Committee would not exceed the estimates. As to the deputation he drew a glowing picture of the benefits to be derived from these pleasant pilgrimages by the deputators who, of course, attended "as many lectures as they could." He added that from the Edinburgh exeur- sion last year they came back with a fall report, and Qn Councillor Heaton' interposing that he bad heard nothing of the report, the Alderman blandly retorted that that was because the report was a serious matter. If it had been ot a highly frivolous character,. he imagined that Couneillor Heaton would have remembered all about it. After this the amendment was put, and it was found that there were only Councillors Hutchinson and Hill to endorse it. As there were seventeen votes on the other side. the minutes were, of course, con- firmed.

In submitting the minutes of the Sanitary Work Committee, Councillor Monks entered into some details as to the estimates which did not differ materially from those of last year. Tnere was, however, one satisfactory piece of information in the councillor's statement. The demand for the product of Longford is increasing, and the sales are larger, and he hinted that in the future they might go in for a better price. Councillor Muir again figured as a- critic, making the somewhat bold assertion that each of the three committees among which the duties of the old Sanitary Committee had been apportioned spends as much as the united committee formerly did. Councillor Roberts at once challenged this rather startling insinuation. lie conceded that Councillor Muir is an authority on finatice, and when the councillors seemed dis- posed to enjoy this as a joke at Councillors Muir's expense, Mr. Roberts preferred he could not under- stand why they should smile so audibly. At any rate whether Councillor Muir was an authority in finance or not he was wrong in his conclusions this time. The change had not led to greater expendi- ture but it had secured greater efficiency. A dispo- sition was then shown by Alderman Sutton to rub off an old score against Councillor Hutchinson re the matter of deputations. The worthy councillor was now, remarked the Alderman, posing as a care- Jul economist in respect to deputations, but it was not that way two or three months ago, when the committee of which he (Councillor Hutchinson) is the chairman proposed that a deputation should go to London, and see the new fire engine painted --or was it to see the new fire engine before it was painted? Ciuncillor Hutchinson seemed just a little hurt by this reap- ing up of bye-gones,and he wanted the Chairman to declare the Alderman out of order, but after all the spoken vtrord cannot be withdrawn, and there seemed to, be a feeling that the Alderman had made a palpable hit.

The proceedings over the Paving and Sewage Committee, and the School Attendance Committee were not discursive. The proposal of the first- named Committee, that instead of employing their own carters and horses they should go in, through the medium of a contractor, for the cheapest men and the cheapest material in the shape of horse flesh, was agreed to without a protest. In moving the minutes of the Museum Committee, Councillor Roberts referred to the nig- gardly fashion in which the County Council treated Warrington in regard to grants in aid of technical education. He pointed out, that Warrington received much less than it was 'entitled to, and than it would receive if it were a county borough. It was the largest non-county borough in England, and he hinted that it might be necessary to alter the present state of things by taking steps to have the town made a county borough, a dignity to which its population now entitled it.

div.head: WEEKLY REPORT ON THE HEALTH OF WARRINGTON.
div.p: WEEKLY REPORT ON THE HEALTH OF WARRINGTON.

During the week, which was the 12th of the current year, the following births and deaths were registered :—Births : Warrington, 38 ; Latchford, 3 ; total,4l. Deaths: Warrington, 20; Latchford, 4; total 24. The excess of births over deaths was 17. The death-rate from all causes was equal to 222 per 1,000, against 20.1 the average of the previous tour weeks, and against 11.3 the corresponding week of last year. The deatb..-rate from the seven chief zymotic diseases was Aunt to 31 per 1,000, against 3,9 the average rate of the four previous weeks, and Against 0.9 the corresponding week of 1893. The ages of mortality were :-0 to 1, 8 ; 1 to 5,1; 5 to 15,1; 15 to 25, 2 ; 25 to 60, 9 ; 60 up 3; total, 24. The deaths included-1 from enteric fever; 1 from measles ; 2 from whooping cough ; 2 from puerperal fever; 1 from croup; 1 from phthisis ; 1 from ancernia ; 4 from lung disease ; 2 - from heart disease ; 2 from kidney disease; 2 from brain disease. The following cases of infectious dis- eases have been reported during the week :—Erysi- pelas 1; scarlet fever, 3; enteric I; puerperal fever, 3. Patients in Hospital 24 March, 26. METEOROLOGY.—The mean temperature was 43.5 Fah., and therefore 21 deg. higher than the preced- ing week. The maximum temperature 61 F., was t recorded on the 24th inst., and the minimum temperature 28 F., on the 18th inst. The rainfall measured nil inch. The general direction was Easterly, the reading of the Anemometer denoting 1,200 miles.—JOHN 11. GORNALL, Medical Officer ot 'Leath.

div.head: BEFORE Til E MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE Til E MAGISTRATES

YOUTHFUL PILFERERS. 1 At the Warrington Borough Court on Saturday morn- ing three bays named Griffith Roberts (10), Henry Roberts (8), and George Elis (8), were chargael with stealing a quantity of timber, value 6d. from Messrs. J. Crosfield and S )ns' soap works. Police-constable Lewis found the boys near the works, carrying the tim- ber. He sent the two emaller boys home, but detained the bigger one, who was miserably clad and extremely dirty. The officer purchased some bread and tea for the boy, and this he ate as if he had been starving. The Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children was communicated with, and their inspector (Mr. Uphill) visited his home, and found it comparatively well fur- nished and clean. Griffith Roberts, however.very often slept out all night. and gave .his parents great trouble.— Regarding the theft, John Marsh, timekeeper, at Messrs. Crosfield's, identified the wood produced as the property I of the firm. There were numerous robberies from the works, and the firm did all they could to discover the offenders. There were so many exits at the works that it was difficult to discover the thieves.—The Clerk : But cannot you alter that state of things by reducing the number of exits P—Witness : Not very well, sir. Mr. Crosfleld is anxious that your worships should make an example of these offenders when they come before yell. because they give us a great deal of trouble and anxiety —The Chairman : Is there no method that presents itself to your m'ard by which you could prevent this pilfering ? Could not the premises be guarded in some way 2—Witness ;We cannot very well get to the vari- ous departmet,ts, as the works are scattered about.— The Chairman : Y.n must try to devise some me hod to prevent little ehiliren like these being brought before the Bench. You owe it to yourselves and to the public to make better arrangemente to prevent this pilfering going on. Henre'llaberts and Ellis will be discharged ; Griffith Roberts will receive six strokes of the birch rod, and be detained in the bririprp-11 for several hours.

SOLDIERS' ESCAPADE. Two soldiers, Thotnas Reid,- and John SulEvan,' stationed at Orford Barracks were charged at the Warrington Borough Police Court on Tuesday morning with stealing on Friday evening, a horse and trap, harness, whip and rag, valued £3O, the property of Thomas tinswortk 3 Buttermarkea street. The Chief Constable sated that on Friday evening at 91.5, Henry • Andrews, the errand boy of ThornasUnsworth, had been out with the horse and trap,and returned to his master's shop to take out a basket. When he came out again a few minutes later he saw that the horse and trap were missing. Infortra,: inn was given to the police and they telephoned to various parts of the country, and the two prisoners were captured by P.C. Lowe at Patricroft bridge, th same night at arlut, eleven o'clock. They were brought back to Warrirgton the next morning by Detective Monaghan, and when charged they said that they did not intend to steal the trap.—Thonias tins- worth and Henry Andrews on being called said that they icientiEedrhe trap and other articles.—P.C. Lowe said that in consequence of information he received he was on the look out for the missing horse and trap, and caught the prisoners at Pa-sicroft bridge. They were then slightly nutter the influence of drink. When he stopped them, they told him that they had hired the trap in Salford, and were then returning. Witness however took them to te Patricioft police station, from whence they were taken next morning by Det‘ntive Monaghan. After evidence by Detective Monaghan, the prisoners were a-ked if they had anything to say. Reid said that he had had a little drop of drink in his head,but he had no intention of stealing the horse and trap. and Sullivan said that they took the horse away with the intent;nn of taking it back. They did not know how far taey had got, but they did not intend to go outside Warrington. Prisoners were committed to Liverpool Quarter Sessions. PENSIONERS AND THEIR PENSIONS.

FOO rBALL.
FOUNTAINS IN PLAY.

Who doesn't enjoy looking at a fountain in play ? The bright water leaps into the air as though it were a living conscious thing. Then at the summit of its arch it is shattered into spray" by the wind, or wafted to and fro like the skirts .of a dancing girl. And all the while the roar of Its rush and the tinkling melody of its fall, fill the air. This is water having a good time—water in high spirits. What trukes it jump, sing, and laugh in that fashion ? Wait a bit. It you ph aie, we will have the explanation later on. Perhaps you know already : perhaps not. It isn't so easy to know things from the bottom.
