WARRINGTON v. WIDNES.

Warrington met Whines on Saturday at the Lower, heuse Lane enclestire, - and showed how inconsistent their play is at times, by sustaining a defeat. The many counter attractione had had their effect upon the big gate which generally aseeinbles at Widnes, for there was hardly a couple of thousand spectators on the field. The (ley was decidedly unsuited to foothill. for the summer-like heat naturally had a detrimental effect upon the performances of both teams. Warrington were minus the services of Jolley, James Beta, Taylor and Thorniley. The teams 'sere of the following composition :—War- Anton : Heeeme, back ; Massey, Carey, Cross, and Broady, t awe-quartert hicks; Evans and John Bate (cap- tain), half hacks; Nevins, Dakin.Berry,Hampson,Bailey, Randies, Higham, and Burrows, forwards. Widnes : Brennan, back ; Rispan, Hughes, Claske, and Dunba- vand, three-quarter backs ; Barber and Drummond, half backs; Gordon, Aldford, Foster, Ridgway, Fraser, Hogan, Darbyshire, and Emery, forwards. Barber kicked off, and the first heeena took place an the War- rington twenty-five. A h)fty kick by Cross was well followed up by Carey, and a deeperate race to the line saw Brennen just-- defeating the visitor, and kicking dead. The drop-out saw' Warrington still aggressive, and although Crese accepted a. pass his kick did not avail his side much, for Brennan easily cleared, and the Widues forwards rushine•the scrimmages EleeSurn saved daringly at the half-Way flag. Cross and Broady beat the Widnesians back, and then game a drop at goal by Massey, the attempt • Wling-short. A penalty kick against the visitors was .*el utilized, but Hampson, Neville, and Berry led'the way back to the Widnes bee, the firstanamee. floorinClatke. Rispan. .next tried a drop at goat witheet soedesseevhilst Carey and Brennan 'exchanged, end Heesona 'put- a finiAli to the bout' by find- ' ing touch at hall-was'. Dakin, Burrows., and Higham were the leacrecs irealorniiidable rush, whilst Hampson • and Ramiles Were dribbling neatly. when Rispan saved well. The Widnes half backs again got the better of the visiting pair, and a good. run by Drummond was fol- lowed by Forster lefing. held under the posts. , Clarke next made an effort, but Broady was more thS.n a match. Nevins, Dakin, and Berry were next leaders in a rush which gave Brennaa trouble, but Barber cleared -(eat the invaders, and Hughes was the means of placing the game once more at the Wairington quarter flag. Heesom wae loudly applauded fora fine save,whilst Hughes in try- ing to round his opponents failed to clear Raisin. Broady next dribbled splendidly along the reserved touch, and actually pissed Brennan, but Barber's tine turn of speed saved the home line from disaster. Evans had a splendid opening but preferred to pass, whilst the next movement saw Massey making. a reckless dash for the oval, and the chance was not only missed, but the payer injured. Brennan saved, and following the drop out Clarke raced away, but Broady once more easily accounted for him. fligham made a brilliant attemptto get through, but found .the tackling safe, whilst good work by Aid ford and Drummond gave Heesom trouble, play settling down at the centre flag. A rush headed by Foster was well met ny Bate, and although Heesom got the sphere away Brennan kicked judiciously, and Wid- nes maintained the attack. A minor was next chronicled to-the locals, but Evans ,and Bate passed, and play was getting dangerously near the , Widnes lines when Clarke picked up in the twee and looked a certain scorer until Broady pulled him up. A penalty kick was then given the Widnes men in front of the Warrington pests, but Drummond failed at the eaV place, and Evans got the leather beyond the half-way flag. Twice in quick suc- cession were the home team penalised, hut Brennan and Hughes defended well. The Widnes forwards rucked the scrimmages in vigorous fashion, and although Broady stayed one in fine style, another attempt headed by Fostur culminated in that player. scoring at the cor- ner. - Widnes again presented a hold front soon after the unsuccessful kick at goal, for Broady had a kick charged. However near the close Warrington made a b6ld bid to draw level, but found the defence true in every detail, and the conclusion of a hard-fought game was a victory for Widnes by a try to nil.

• Under date of March 16th 1892, a lady writes that for twenty years she always felt low-spirited. Now what is meant by " spirits" in this sense, is a condition of the mind in respect of our being cheerful, happy, enjoy- ing our surroundings, taking delight in all sorts of minor matters, and, in a word, making the most of life our- selves and helping othersto make the most of it. Well, then, it is both a glorious and a profitable thing to be always in good spirits ; I wish I could be myself. But I can't ; anyhow I'm not. Neither is anybody. Yet why not? What makes our hearts sink down like plummet, and then rise like a cork ? Before we answer let us read the rAt`of Vie letter. The writer says : " For twenty years I have suffered from liver complaint and indigestion. I was constantly tired, weak, and languid. My skin was a stilovv colour and I had great pain at the back and shoulders. .

"My appetite was poor, I had a bad taste in the - month, and much pain and weight at the chest after eating,. I was also frequently sick, throwing up a sour frothy fluid. I took different kinds of medicine, but none of them gave me reliefond I got weaker andweaker "In March, 1884, I became so bad that I called a doctor, who attended me MT and on for twelve months. He gave me medicines but I grew no better, as nothing he prescribed seemed to reach my complaint. About this time I heard of Mother Seigel:s Syrup, and com- menced taking it. In less than a'month all my pain and distress ceased, a ndl have sinca,bien in good health. .1 keep a bottle of the Syrup in the house as a fl.mily medi- cine, and 11 taking an occasional dose have needed no doctor.

"I may mention that my aunt, who lives at West - Wycombe, • Bucks, was nfflicted with indigestion and dyspepsia. She states that in her opinion, Mother Seigel's Syrup has been the means of saving her life. You are at liberty to use this statement as you may see fit. Yours truly, (Signed) Mrs, Harriet Cutler, Burton .House, 33, Kenmure-road, Hackney, London.' No philosopher has yet been able to say what is the exact relation of the mind to the body. This much, however. experience constantly assures us of ; that it is very intimate, and that the condition of the mental

faculties 'depends upon that of the body. As birds sing when the sun Alines, and are dumb in the dark, So the spirit 3 and mental power, rise and express themselves when we, are in hr.talth, and are dull and torpid when the body is under the weight of pain and disease. And. to know that is to know all we re quire to act upon.

Everything, money, influence, and every form of suc- cess depends so largely upon health that by universal consent we don'texpect good service fromthose whoare ill And illness, nine times in ten, means precisely what Mrs. Cutler suffer-id from such a long and weary period —indigestion and dyspepsia—the ailm eat cured, (when the doctors are done with their fruitless experiments) by Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup. The fountains play only when the water is forced powerfully through their pipes by gravity or by machinery. So the spirits are free and elastic only when the organs within us act without hindrance or obstruction.

WARRINGTON " A " Y. WIDNES "A."—.This match was played at Warrington on Saturday,before a small "gate.". Warrington started the leather,and after the combatants had got settled down some capital passing between Cox, Tuhoy and Peters carried the warfare to the home lines, the home team being lucky in escaping with a minor al. er a couple of kicks being charged, A strung rush by Frerth, Wilcox, Knight,and Forster Was only checked on the line. Some mulling allowed the Widnesians to clear and transfer the contest to the Warrington quarters, but Boscow was alive to the danger. The Warrington for- warth were playing very well and caused their opponetits some anxiety, and after some smartness by Mason and Lally the visiting forwards dribbled to half way, where one of the Widnes forwards twisted his leg and had to retire. This was followed by the Chemicals attacking, and from a inisun&rstanding between two backs Widnes got a " soft " try near the posts and kicked a goal. After the restart Owen was prominent:, and _Lawless, .jun., supplemented by smart kicking. Upon the resumption of hostilities after half-time Warrington attacked, hut Higlifield tricked his opponents and got beautifully away to -thidfield. Good kicking between

Cunningham, dra.yson and Lawless was succeeded by Widnes emulating their previous display, and a magni- ficent bout o: passing by their team was ttly checked in time by the smartness of Warrington. Boscow relieved and tnen 4 nice bp of work by Mann, Lally and Gibson was responded t. 4 by Peters making a fine Andging run to centre. Forster, Knight, Freerh and Litherland dribbled the ball hack co the Widnes 25, but Widnes retaliated until a rush by Lawles:,Wilc-ix and Woodward carried 'he labor to the line, and a smart bit of play between Law!, as, jun.. nannion and Cunningham forced Widnes to kick dead. L twless, jun., replied splendidly to the drop•our, and from loose work on the line, Cun- ningham got a try, but no goal was kicked. Warrington were now having the best of matters, Lawless, jun., as extra half-back being very energutic, but although Warrington a'most scored on one. occasion, Widnes retired victors of a good and enjoyable game by 1-0-2 to 0-1-2.

RUNCORN V. WIGAN.—An exciting contest was de- 1 cided on Saturday afternoon between these two teams , on the Irwell-htne enclosure, Runcorn. 'I here was a 1 large " gate " and the weather was all that could be de- I sired. The homesters began operations and immediately began to press. Their opponents maintained a capital defence and gave very few chances. At length the visi- tors invaded the Runcornians citadel,and some difficulty was experienced in driving them to the centre of the ' venue. Play continue ,1 in this situation for some time, but eventually the Cheshire men became the masters, and again threatened the ‘Vigan " sticks." The defence, however, was impregnable arid all efforts of the home men to score proved unavailing. flalf•time arrived and nothing had been notched. In the secodd half the visit- ing team seemei si,m,,what ezhausted and allowed Run- corn to gain the nffer,sive. Their backs were, how- ever, very reliable and prevented any scoring. On several occasions the home team looked like gaining a victory but inet with very hard lines. The game elided Runcorn nil, Wigan nil. lityscont4 "A" v. WIGAN " A " TnAms.—The Runcorn juniors paid a visit in IVigan on Saturday afternoon and engaged in an encounter before a numerous attendance cut spectators and in beautiful weather. Runcorn in the first half had all the best of the play, and were success- ful in notching three points to their opponent a nil. Upon the resumption of hostilities Wigan showed better form • and from a penalty kick Halton scored a goal. Some pod tackling was witnessed after this success, both team.; doing their utmost tl improve matters but their • efforts wee in vain. At the call of time the score sto,d Runcorn one try, three points ; Wigan, one penalty goal. three points.

THEFTS FROM THE—NLCRICET.—AIexander Potts, Tilley- st., and William Mostyn, Gee-st., two youths, were charged with stealing from a stall in the Market-place, belonging to Mr. William Beswick, a quantity ol matches, straps, Ste. in all of the value .of 24.—The Chief Constable stated that at half-past six o'clock that morning Constable Barnett saw the prisoners in the Market Shed sto.aping down and acting in a Ruspicious manner. He caught hold of Potts, who had 28 boxes of matches, five pairs of laces, and three pairs of leather straps in his pockets. On Mostyn he found 15 boxes of matches, and other articles, keys being found on both. All the articles, except a tin of milk, had bees identified by Mr. Beswick as his property.. Mr. Beswick, who is a general dealer in Buttermark.4-st., and who also has a stall in the market, said the articles were safely locked up in the stall on Wednesday night. The prisoners fsal they found the articles lying about the market. They had not stolen thcm.—They were fined 10s. and costs each, or 14 days' imprisontrent.

MONDAY.—Before Messrs. J. Brundrit and A. Themes, LICENSE TRANSFER.—The Bench granted the tempor- ary transfer of the license of the" Shamrock" Inn. Regent-street, from Samuel Silcock to James Hunt. AN OCCASIONAL LICENSE GRANTED.—An application was made by George Itiley,Bridge lon, Ashbridge-street for an occasional license to Fell intoxicants from 2 to 10 o'clock p.m. on the football field, on the 7th inst. the eccasion being the Brass Band Contest.—No objection was made by Superintendent Atherton, and the per- mission was granted. CHAEGE OF COAL STEALING. —A boy named John Rue, twelve years of age, and livisig in Water-street was charged with stealing ten lbs of coal valued is. on the 24th March the property of the M.S.C. Coy.—P.C. Lee deposed to seeing the ixiy come from the direction of the Ship Canal Works with a bag containing coal and coke. On being questioned by the officer he said it had been given to him by another boy.—Dismissed. A CYCLIST WITHOUT A LWElT.—Percy Buckley was fined. including costs for 'riding a bicycle in Halton- road on the evening of the 17th March without a lamp. USING 08-CENE LANGUAGE —Ann Corcorran, for this offence on the 23rd March in Brunswick-street,was fined we. and crests or fourteen days. A Lerree STRRET low.—Martin Gilligan of Cooper-st., was summoned for having assaulted George Sefton, a resident of the same street, on the 20th March.—Prose- cutor stated that on the Sunday night, at about ten o'clock, he wai passing dawn rover street when he heard some persona shouting and screaming. On reach- ing the scene of the disturbance he saw a lot of men and women abusing a woman. The defendant was amongst the men, and when he (witness) said it was a shame that so many persons should be abusing one woman, the defendant struck him a severe blow in the mouth.— Defendant denied having struck the complainant. ' The evidence brought by both parties proved most conflict- ing.—At length the magistrates imposed refiner)! 10s. and costs against the defendant with an alternative of fourteen days hard labeur. DISORDERLY TOPERS.—John Edwards was fined ss. for being drunk and disorderly in High-street, on the 31st ult.—For similar misconduct John Lydia and Martin Flaherty were each tweeted in fines of 55. STEALING AND " BECElVlNG."—Blizabeth Beers, was charged with qeeling on the 31st March, a silk hand- kerchief, valued 3e 3d., the property of John Ackerley, 38, Halt-en-road, and Steven and Ellen Nicholls were each charged with having received the same whilst knowing it to have been stolen.—Annie Ackerley, wife of the prosecutor, deposed to the handkerchief being missed from the shop window at 10 30 on Saturday night. It had been pinned to a shirt but at the time named, the pin alone remained in the shirt supporting the theory that the handkerchief had been pulled away. div.head: STARVING IN THE STREETS.
div.p: STARVING IN THE STREETS.

About nine o'--cick on Wednesday night the St. Helens police found a man lying in Warrington New-road, in that town, in an unconscious condition. He was at once carried on the ambulance to Dr. McNicoll's surgery, and from there to the hospital, where he remained in the same condition during the night. On Thursday, how- ever, there was a change, and he stated that his name was John Ward, thirty-nine years of age, a military tailor, of Stratford, and -hal been in the Army for thirty years. He had been at Belfast.and came across to Fleet- wood on Friday night, having a had passage. He came by train to St. Helens, but had no recollection of how he came to be in Warrington-road or what had happened to him. Mr. Jameson (assistant to Dr. M'Nicoll) visited the hospital on Thursday morning, and he expresses the opinion that it was a case of starvation and phthisis.

div.head: ST. HELENS CONVICTS.
div.p: THE ST. HELENS CONVICTS.
A GRUESOME SIGHT.

On Tueseliy Frank Riley, one of the St. Helens con- victs, had another interview with his relatives, this time his wile, two of his children—Thomas aged nine, years, and the yoengest eighteen months old—and his mother-in-law, Mrs. Smith, visiting Walton Gaol. On meeting iu the room set apart for visitOr3 all the parties burst into tears, and it wae some time before they ceuld check their emotion. Thomas put the question," When are you coming home, daddy ?" to which the prisoner, had to reply," I don't know." Mrs. Riley stated last ' night to our St. Helens representative that she scarcely knew her °husband at first he was so much altered. He however, tried to be cheerful, after the tears had sub- sided, and said he was glad to see her and the cliiidren. He was afraid it meant a life sentence to !jib'. Some of the prisoners had told him so, but he hoped it would not be so bad. He would he thankful if God spared him to come home again to his children. He- expressed grateful thanks to , those who bad worked successfully for a reprieve. He mentioned a gruesome sight which he witnessed on the previous day, before the execution of Mrs. Waller. He ' was looking through the grating in his cell across the prison yard. He saw Mrs. Walber walk arross the yard assisted by two female warders. She leoked y( ry bad indeed, and it made his blood run ccld,ar,d he shuddered all over when he thought of the fate which was await- ing her, and which he had narrowly eseaued. Be also saw the hangsman go through the 'aril with a small strap in his hand, and he could stand it no longer, and had to get down. He repeated that he was innocent of the crime and never struck the constable at all. He begged of his wife to look after his five children, .and trail* them up well. •During the interview the younger child repeatedly called out" Daddy," and wanted to get to the wire netting which separated the efisoner from the visit4rs. Riley motioned kisses with his hand, and appeared much affected.

OCCASIONAL LICIZNSER GRANTED. SINGULAR PROCEEDINGS.

At St. flelens, on Tuesday, before Alderman M'Bryde and Mr. W. J. Thompson, Mr. Massey made application on behalf of Mr. Charles Liptrot, licensee of the Beehive hotel, for occasional licenses to sell intoxicating liquor at the St. Helens football matches against Swititm on Thursday night and Warrington on Saturday afternoon. He said the ground was a long distance from the town, and numbers of per- sons would visit St. Helens to witness the matches. He submitted that in a matter of that sort the only ques- tion to be considered was the comfort and convenience of the public, and it was only natural that refreshment would be required. Occasional licenses should be granted on occasions like football matches. In the interests of the public it was desirable that they should be granted. Mr. Massey raised a further contention, that under the Act of Par;iament. 26 and 27 Victoria, it only required the consent of one magistrate. He mentioned the fact that similar applications had been refused three times previously, but he said it was as much in the hands of the bench to make a departure from one magistrate who had been the cause of the refusal as it was for that one tnaOstrato to make a &Torture from the recognised rust iii of the bench for twenty years. The application always been granted previously. The magistrates retired, a•,(1 alter consulting for fifteen minutes, re- turned neo court—Mr. Thompson then said : I grant the a pialicati,.n.—The Chairman (Alderman M'Bryde) did not ma ke any remarks.

CONCILIATION IN TilE COAL TRADE.
THE "LIVING WAGE" NEGATIVED.

A meeting of the Coal Trade Board of C,,eciliation was held on Tuesday in London. Lord Shand, the chair- man chosen by the Speaker. presided, He referred to the responsibility of his position, to the important ques- tions about to be discussed, and earnestly pointel out that the true meaning of conciliation was concession. He urged that both coalowners' and miners' representa- tives should go as far as possible in the path of s'incilia- tion, so that they might ultimately hit upon a solution of the great vestiosis; they had to determine. Their deliberations, he said, should be characterised by frank- ness, by freedom from concealment and deceit. looked upon the Board as a great experitrieet. Their proceedings were being watched with interest on the Cantinent, and it would be a humiliation if they did not succeed in their object. Mr. A. M. Chambers, for the coalowners, and Mr. Fickare, for the miners, expresmed their confidence in his Lordship's impartiality and their desire to arrive at a satisfactory settlement. A corres- pondent states that the rules setting forth the objects of the Board of Cenciliation were adopted. qn the pro- posal for fixing a minimum wage the two parties on the Bard were equally divided, and Lord Shand gave his casting vote against the minimum wage. He explained, however, that his attitude must not be taken as express- ing any opinion on the principle. He had simply ob. jected to the inclusion of the minimum wage as a rule. A meeting of the Executive of the Miners' Federation was held in London on Wednesday. The proceedings were private, bet it is stated that the position of the Federation as affected by the decisions of Lord Shand at the previous day's wittlng'of the, Conciliation Board was discussed. '

div.head: DENONNCINO LORD SHAND.
div.p: DENONNCINO LORD SHAND.

At a meeting of miners at Nottingham on Thursday evenirg Councillor Bailey, Notts r iners' agent and a representative of the miners on the Conciliation Board, said their leaders were not wise when they accepted the Rosebery agreement. They accepted Lord Shand in good faith, but by his first decition he had prov.-d him- self to be a hiasse4l and prejudiced partisan. When, an hour alter taking the chair, his Lordship swept away the main plank of the miners' platform, the miners' leaders were justified in withdrawing their confidence from him. Rather than allow a 111311 of that character to decide whether wages should be reduced they would fa,:•,e all the horrors of the struggle they had la,tely gone tkrough. Councillor Bailey went on to describe Lord Shand as either asham or a hypocrite, and urged that his powers should be limited. A resolution declaring Lord Shand a biassed rartisan and unfitted for the Post was unanimously carried.

ST. JOHN'S CHURCH CHOIR.

The members of the above choir, were entertained ,16% tea in the Parochial Mio4oll ils;I, Harlestown, on zibssday eA.enirg by the WI,. T. R. Matthews, vicar. About 25 sat down to tea, aftor which various *tatters reganiing the reconstruction of the choir, Were discussed, this becoming neressary in cone& ailteace of the appointment of Mrs. Latimer, as S-f 11„ aa st, in plus., ot Mr Wsek,. The remainder of me evening was spent in games and dancing. TH.B REDISTRIBUTION OF COUNTY COURT DISTRICTS.

,eThe memorial ot the.Haydock LOSal Board pray- etiB for a redistribution of County Court juriadic- 'Mk so that Hay dock would come within the St. flelens circuit instead of Warrington as at present as been presented by the Hon. T. W. Legh, the Newton Division, to the bard Chancellor. Mr. J. W. Green. solicitor, St. Helens, acted on be- of Haydock tradesmen who desired a change, tul it was chiefly owing to his exertions that the ilaydock Local Board decided tA move in the matter. APPOINTMENT OF A TRAINED NURSE AT EARLESTOWS. some time ago toe Committee of the Medical Aid e 'moiety decided to engagi a trained nurse, and ap- Deiced a sub-committee to look into the matter. A eiew days ago a general committee meeting was 'meld to receive the report of he sub-committee, Who recommended the engagement of Nurse Wil- , the, formerly matron at Hay dock Cottage Hospital. he general committee approve.' he recommenda- . time of the sub-committee, and Nurse Wilson will later upon her duties on Tuesday next. Certain *les drawn up by the sub-committee were very , telly discussed, amended, and adopted. The minis- . liers, city missionaries, and medical men, are the sigy members of the committee through whom the Services of the nurse can be obtained. GOOD TEMPLARS. The weekly Session of the Hope of Barlestown Lodge of Good Tempters was held in the Co-opera- 'e Hall, Ear lestown, on Monday evening. Bro.G. . 11. Waehurton, t.-%T., presided, and there was a good attendance, including 17 visitor+ from the Great ' tfeart, Lodge, St. Helens, and Bro. Q.M. Sergt. 'Roberts, of Warrington. Two candidates were in- vited. After the usual business. Sister Mrs. Frances Presided and the various offl !t•4 were taken by the visitors. An excellent programme of songs, recite- , binnEe fee. was rendered by the visitors. An address 'was given by Bro. Roberts. In a few practical re- - *arks Bro. G. E. Warburton proposed a vote of Illsanks to the visitors, widen Wr.B seconded by Bro. • W. Jameson, a'r-id supported by Bret+. Newman, Starke, Willis and responded to by Bro. Frances. CONFIRMATION SERVICE AT NEWTON. The Right Rev. Dr. Reyston, a-sistant Bishop of Liverpool, attended at St. Peer's Cuurch, Newton, •11 Friday afternoon for the purpo-e of performing the usual confirmation ceremony to candidates from 1:42e parishes of Wargrave, Lowton. and St. Peter's, , Aevstori. The candidates, of whom there were 70 both sexes, were in charge of the Rees. +T. Carson (Wargravel, J. Smith (Lowton). and H. Monk and Ir. W. Johnstone, St. Peter's. There were a large *Umber of people present at the service. Previous to the ceremony of laying on of blends, the bishop delivered an address of con- , aiderable length to the candidates, which embodied , 410 me very excellent advice, as to their conduct in life, in the course of which he referred particularly h the value of reading good literature. THE HEALTH OF EIAYDOOS. The medical officer of Hitydoce (in.. Hayward), in resenting his quarterly repert, oii Thursday, said *e health of the township was eery satisfactory. Tkere had been seventy-seven births and twenty- 'ht deaths, giving a death rate of 15.5 per 1,000 Per annum, which was exceptionally low. There had only been one death from zymetic diseases,and tewenty-three notifications' of sickness. The Local ; zoard decided to adopt the Public Health Amend- : *out Act. In accordance with the general order ef the Local Government Board, 1891, it was decided - to re-appoint a medical officer ac t ia+ next meeting. eclie Local -Board had increased the salary of Dr. ,aLaywa, and they applied to the C .unty Council a portion of the salary to be refunded. NEWTON BOARD OF COMIIISSIONERS.

The monthly meeting of the Newton Board of Commissioners was held at the Earlestown Town Hall, on Monday afternoon. There were present: Mr. J. W. Emmett (inthe chair), Col. Nlceryrquodale and Messrs. T. Ormand, G. Ratcliffe, J. Smith, T. McMahon, P. Thompson. E.T. Evans, T. Forster, Cillingwood, J. B. Worslev (law clerk), R. Brierley (surveyor), and Dr. Watkins (medical officer of health).

GAS AND WATICR COMMITTEE. At a Meeting of this Committee held on Monday, March 19th, the gas manager's report was read and instructions given to him to obtain the remainder of the cannel due under contract, before the end of June. The carbonizing account for the past month was: fuel used, 229 tons, 5 owt. ; gas made 3,308,100 feet, being an average of 10.039 feet per ton of fuel used. Messrs'. Emmett and Ormand were appointed to look into the system of keeping the gas works accounts and bo, ki. Mr. Swan was instructed to inquire into the prepaynient water system in other towns.—The minutes were adopted.

TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION COMMITTEE. At a meeting of this Committee it was decided to grant £6O from the Commissioners' general improvement account in aid of the expenses of the Technical Instruc- tion Committee, for the ensuing session.—The minutes were confirmed.

FINANCIAL COMMITTYK. The minutes of this Committee stated that at a meet- ing held on March 19th, Mr. James Smith, as successor to Mr. Gillespie, was elected chairman of the Finance Committee. An application from Mr. Houghton for increase of salary was again considered and it was resolved that the application should be deferred until examined into further. It was decided that the rent, fire, gas and attendance at the new office; should be apportioned: to the highway department, £5O; school attendance, £25 ; gas, £25; water, £25; and highways sanitary department, £25 yearly. Cheques were signed for payment to the amount of £1,835 93.—The minutes were warmed.

HIGHWAYS COMMITTER. At a meeting of the Highways Committee 7,-,eld on the 22nd March Mr. Brierley submitted an offer of the Main Roads Committee of the County Council of £llOO for repairs and spscial grants for the year ending March 1895. It was resolved that the offer should be accepted on the understanding that £l5O only be expended on reforming the roadway across tho Common. Messrs. Ratcliffe, Forster and McMahon were appointed a sub- committee to inspect and report on the advisibility of providing stabling and additional horses , for, highways and other work of the Committee. The following bilild- ing plans were submitted and approved: Thomas Stn- derson, coach-house, stables awl lofts, off Cri-ss-l-ne ; Richard Jones, four houses and shop, Wargrtve New. ; Mrs. Mary Boardman, two houses in St. Helens- road; John Lea, live housas in ,St. Helens-r.ad ; and Messrs. W. Hafson, F. Buck, and H. Starkie, six houses in St. Helens-road (conditionally). MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT. , Dr. Watkins (medical officer of health) submitted his quarterly report from which it appeared that 1 the total number of births in the district in that period had been 121, and deaths 36. Considering the increase in the number of births the infantile mortality had been un- usually small, while the death-rate generally was one of the lowest in Ilngland.—Mr. Smith said this spoke very well for the excellent sanitary conditions of the town.

DIVISION OF TIM DISTRICT INTO WARDS. Mr. Worsley said he had received from the County Council an order confirming the decision come to at the recent enquiry for the division of the district into wards. There would be five wards, and the number of repre- sentatives on the Commissioners would be increased from ten to fifteen, three members being elected from each ward. The election under these new conditions would take place in November, and ancording to rul,s to be prescribed by the County Council. In 1895 1 he-en would be no election, but during the three succeeding years five members would retire each year.—The in- struction was adopted as favourable. This concluded the business of the meeting.
ST. JOHN'S 04.111taH, EAItLESTOWN.

The annual congregational tea meeting and enter- tainment in connection with St. John's Churcll took place on Monday evening, in the Parochial Mission 'Hall. About .£2O had been, subscribed in trays, which is much above any other previous occasion, and upwards of 300 persons were present to tea, which was very much enjoyed, the tables being presided over by the tray gtvers. After tea the attendance was much augmented, there being folly 400 present. The following programme was then pro- ceeded with and carried through with excellent taste and finish :—Piano solo, Mrs. Latimer,song," At the Ferry,” Miss Conway, song. " Grace Darling," Miss flarcif4, song, " Love's request," Mr. Monks, song, "Faith and truth," Miss Hatch, song, " Maegie," Miss. A Clark“.. song, The Better way," Miss Conway, quartette " 0 who will o'er the Downs," Misses Tripp and Ma:ll'ex, -Messrs. Monks and Mayhew. -At this point the Rev. T. R. Matthews addressed a few pastoral remailts to the congregation, alluding to the losses which they had sus- tained during the year, and spoke in gratit)..ing terms of the numbcr of people who had come amongst them, and whom he hoped they would be able to keep. Speak- ing of the children he told- the parents he should like them to take a htle mats pains to help the teacher.; in the day and Sunday schools. The children in the pree,ent generation, he thought. were not so well behaved as when he was a boy. (Laughter.) The tendency now- adays was to be men or women before they knew where they were. The teachers could not of course cure all that, and therefore he asked them to help the teach- ers to teach the children to behave 'a little better in church on Sunday, and in the school on week days.' If they sat where he sat, in the chancel, on Sunday, and heard all the talking, shuffiirig, quarrelling. &c.' he was afraid they would not. be so very devotional as they were. On this point be would like to sae a •worctor two, They had gone to some expense in the church in provid- ing kneelersisome people appreciated their kistdilesa very much, as they thought they had bees provided put their feet on, and the church cleaner was very mo h annoyed at it. He wanted parental@ teach their ch I- dren to have more of a Missionary spirit, and nett() he so selfish. If parents would give their children Tonney on Sunday they should tell them what ti do with it, t keep it until they got to church , and then put ir in the collection plate, and they would be able to do very inueit • more work in the parish than they were able to d ) present. He thought for lack of mosey, they were very selfish in.Eariestown, they very seldom did anything for Foreign or Home Missions, but he was sure all of there could do a little more than they did at presere • by prac- tising a little self-denial. He concluded by ask;ng for volunteers for the choir which he said was ahour to ti considerably reconstructed. The second part of the'n- tertainment was then proceeded with, and consigpd a clever exposition of sleight of hand tricki,together wit I an excellent exhibition of shadowgraphy, • which was , thoroughly enjoyed.

ST. HELENS TOWN COUNCIL. GAS-LAMP ADVERTISING. NEW ABATTOIR AND MAII!T SEWER. -- MR. SETON-KA.RR'S DINNER TICKET. The monthly meeting of the Sr. Helens Town Council was held on Wednesday, under the pre- sidency of the Mayor (Alderman Sinclair). The G tq Committee had considered an application from a local firm of clothiers that the Corporation would (treet a lamp in the street opposite their shop with the name f the firm thereon, on condition that they sh uld pay a rent for the lamp, that the lamp should be kept audit at the same times as the ordinary street lamps. ad' the gas consumed should be passed through the firm's meter and paid for by them. The committee r, com- mended that the application shopld be granted, r rid oat the rent to be paid should bel per annum.—aldei mari C. J. Bishop did not know whether that was quite a judicious thing. The Highways' Committee should he consulted before it was done. There was also the generg I question whether it was desirable. If -theyalecided to allow this they might have lamps all over the puce 1. r advertisements.—Alderman J. C. Gamble said the -goes- tion had been discussed on previous occasions. The people would pay for the gas and £1 a year for lighting the lamp. It would help to light up the street, and might be an advantage. The Gas Committee would take care there was no obstructionfr—The matter was referred to the Paving Committee.: Councillor John Forster, chairman of the ifeaPh Com- mittee, referred to the proposed erection of a new abat- toir, and said the committee had for a lone time been called upon to erect some such building. There were slaughter-houses which were overcrowded and some in an insanitary condition, and some were scarcely pass- able. Such places would have to be dealt with by the committee. The cost of the new abattoir would be 23,000. With regard to the new main sewer, which It was de- cided should be done by contract, Councillor thttnn suggested that a clause should be inserted that the un- employed men of St. Helens should be put upon the work.—Councillor Forster said a clause of this descrip- tion could not be inserted, but it was Wiped that a local contractor would secure, the Work.—The minutes were confirmed. Councillor J. Hatton asked for details of rut dry dis- bursements amounting in the aggregate to £9O. Alder- man J. C. Gamble produced a list of items, and read "A dinner ticket for Mr. Seton-Kirr, £1 10s."--Counoilior Hatton (interrupting) said he would have a good fed for LllO3. He (Mr. Hatton) never had a dinner for £1 10s. (Laughter.)—The Mayor said the Municipal C upocar ions at their meeting in London, allowed St. Helens repre- sentatives to ask the borough member to he their git-A, and the Corporation paid for him. The Mayor supposed Mr. Hatton would hardly like them not to piy the till price when their member dined like that.—Mr. shook his head. Mr. Seton-Karr being the Conservative member, and Mr. Hatton one of his strong supporters, the incident caused considerable amusement in the Council chamber.

div.head: TTTE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, APRIL 7, 1894.
div.p: TTTE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, APRIL 7, 1894.
CAIRO-STREET SUNDAY SCHOOL.

RE-UNION OF SCHOLARS. There was a large gathering in; Cairo-street schoolroom on Monday evening on the occasion of a re-union of past and present elder scholars of the Sunday School. The school is one of the oldest in Warrington it having been founded in the year 1788. A number of the old scholars were present on Monday—several of them having travelled from a distance. The schoolroom had been decorated for the occasion, the platforin containing a choice collection of ' flowers and plants. A number of portraits of previous pastors of the church were hanging near the entrance tr.) the congregational parlour, and above the platform was a banner containing the words "Welcome to old friends.' The proceedings commenced with a tea at which a good number sat down. A short adjournment was afterwards made to the chapel, when the organist, Mr. J. M. Muir, A.R.C.0., gave a brief organ recital. On re-assembling in the schoolroom. the proceeoings were presided over by the Rev. W. H. Drummond,B. A., and there were also on the platform Messrs. F. Monks, J.P., C.C.,T. Birchall J.P., J. ReKnowles, Smith Knowles, (Manchester), W. Davenport, W.Travers (Liverpool) and David Chadwick (Liverpool). After the singing of a liyion The CHAIRMAN spoke a few words of welcome. le said he was sure it was gratifying to everyone of them to see that so many had responded to their invitation and that there so many present who were representing many" generations of the school life. (Applause.) He believed from the first, from what he had heard of the past of , Cairo-street Sunday school, that the reunion was bound to he a splendid success, Of course,, it went without saying that the old days at ; Cairo-steeet were much brighter than the present days, and they were thankful for those pleasant old times. He was happy tio say that they had a great many who representedthe workers of , the past days with them that night, and their presence ! was a source of inspiration to them. There were many other old workers whose hearts were with them though they could not have them there in bodily presence. He was glad to be able to tell them that they had received letters from several old workers and from his (the .speaker's)predecessors in the pulpit who were stilt livings (applause.) Mr. Drummond then read letters of creat- ing and reminiscence from the following persons: Mr. William Robson, Rev. Thomas }links, of Clifton, Mrs.. Robert Gaskell, Mrs. Dare ,nee Mica Hannah Noble, Revs H.W. Perris, Rev. Priestley Prime. Rev. Charles Traver, ot Carlisle, Rev. Themes- Henry Bibby, Bishops Court, Downpatriek, Mr. Peter Worrall, alontreal, Mr. Renert Pemberton Indiana, U.5.A.., and the Revs Frank Ks Freestsn, of London. Mr. T. BIRCHALL, J.P., said he had spoken ..from that platform a good many times in his life but he did not think he had stood before an audience in ;that place feel- ing a greater difficulty, and feeling mere overpowered in the recollections which that gathering suggested, than he did that eight. He confessed that to him it was a sort of resurrection to see old faces he had not seen for 30 years, and some perhaps for a considerable time besides, and to grasp hands that once were frequently grasped. When he saw four of his old scholars of 30 years ago in that room, all of them filling, their places well in the world, men who had made their mark and done good work in the world, and were come to compare notes and ask about the old times and the old class, he confessed it was almost more than he. could do to reply to them. He believed that no echool in Warrington had had such an ieflnence on the life of Warrington as had Cairo-street school. He vras'of the opinion that at Cairo-street the first great system of sanitary reform originated, when Philip Carpenter got a number of young men to assise him hi inspecting the homes of Warrington and - then printed and published in the town a report on the insanitary state of the town, and pleaded to the Sanitary Authorities to remedy it. In conclusion, he urged rune menland young women to engage in Sunday schoolwork Mr. F. MONKS, J.P.,C.C., said the memory of 50 years was rather a long one. It was rather more than 50 years since he (the speaker) first entered the school, and be regretted that a young lad he induced to become a scholar of the school at that time was not present with them that night. That lad was Arthur Rathbone. (Ap- plause.) Alluding to the Sunday school workers he said Themes Rinks was not so active a worker in the school as Mr. Bishop was, but iminedi.-ately after hie departure, came a friend of everybody, when in 1647, Philip Car- penter came to be the minister. Ile had not been here very long when a calamity came upon the town, equal in iutensity to the one they passed through last year. It was Mr. Carpe,nter's efforts which gave the stimelus to sanitary reform in Warrington. There was another young man who was not e Unitarian but a strong staunch Churchman and Conservative, who put Philip Carpett• ter's theoretical ideas into practice—for Philip Carpenter did to a certain extentelack practicability. With a white- wash brush ,and a bucket i.his mane--Josiah Whittle —and the teachers of the school used to turn out and whitewash - the yards and cottages, mostly of the Irish people in Buttermarket-st., Bank-st., and locality, a duty lie (the speaker) was certain a great many people would shrink from to- as. They had not such dens now. He was all the more pleased to sive this testimony because in Su - sequent years he had the pleasure to work with Josiah Whittle on the Sanitary Committee, and for a long series , of years, almost bordering on 40 3 ears, Josiah Whittle was in the front rank of sanitary reformers, asd had done for Warrington an incalculable amount at work. The speaker afterwards referred to the establishment of the Mut. nil Improvement Society in connection with the Sunday School. Therp was one other thing he wished to say, and that was to impress upen them the valuent public worship. The sermons - that they got, and sech sermons as ; their old friend. . Richard Filcher used to give, he (the speaker) was quite -certain that they could not sit and listen to such discourses with- out benag all the better for it. It was not for them or him to tell, when tee inspiration of a high and noble thought would flow in, orel3o say what Would be the-out- come cf any such inspiration. Within fifteen feet 'from where he was now standing the inspiration and forma- tion of the Warrington Co-operative Society struck in ; the minds of two young men. (Applause.) They know something of the difficulty of its inception, and they had , been privileged to witness something of the great bless- ings which it had given to the people of Warrington .They might depend epee one thing that the .question of co- operation was not settled yet. (Applause.) There was a time also when the proposal was made for what he (the speaker) called the establishment of an industrial . co-operative society, but owing to the jealously ,and the want of confidence oil the part of the people who were most interested, it fell through. H the question of a living wage was to he settled it was bounct to be settled on the principles while had been •taught in Cairo-st. Chapel to his knowledge for the last 50 years. (Ap- plause.) The only road to success was by self denial and self control, and if only working people would become their- own capitalists by their own self denial, and !own self control, arid would have wisdom to put the manage- ! ment of their affairs in the hands of men who hod the ability, they weld& in hie opinion, arrive at a true gem- Mon of the labour difficulty. Ho was not by any means a Socialist in the sense in which they heard it very often spoken of. But there was no Socialism that would ever develop the world but Christian Socialism and after all Christianity was the deepest and the broadest Socialism the world had ever seen. (Hear. hear.) Mr. WALTiitt TRAVHRS, of Liverpool, also addressed the meeting. Further addreesea were given by Mr S. KnowleseMancheter, Mr. Davenport, and Mr. Chad- wick, Liverpool. The 'musical portion of the prinsalines were welt su.asieee be missE. ilirchall, Misses M. E. fld F. M. Monks, and Mr. Pemberton. Miss Birchen contributed a seelie solo, fer which she received a well msited encore, the Misses Mettles sang a duet and Mr. Pembertoe gave a meritorieos interpretation of the song ...Our Jack's come borne again.' err. Muir, A .15.C.0., was the aceempanis.. mrrting closed withthe of " Auld A mead 'if otaia. 15 (lime co esa T. C Hoilisetweerh, tSte reieretory, for.• the excellent arraegetnerits NI, hint) he had made.

div.head: WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY.

The Warrington Musical , Society gave its final concert for the season before a moderate audience ! in the Gymnasium on Tuesday evening, Gounod's Messe Solonnelle (St. Cecilia), and some miscellane- ous items making•up:the progranime. For the pur- poses of the mass, there was •an orchestra which, though not so complete as ,to do full justice to Gounod's scoring, was in other respects most effi- cient, and the manner in which both the instate. mentaliste and the chortle dealt with the work, re- flects great credit, not only upon their individual and collective capability, but upon Mr. Crossley, the Society's indetatigable conductor, whose painstak- ing training was so clearly evidenced. The " Aguas Dei " • with which the mass was closed,was, so far as the orchestra is concerned,the weakest number,and what wee noticeable was rather a want of neatness and crispness in executing some of the flowing accompaniments, than. the di.movery of any more ;serious difficulty. The " Offertory ' (principally for muted strings), was, on the other hand, just .as meritorious, and in its dreary tranquility :was a most striking antithesis -of the demonstrative " Credo" which immediately preceded it. Gounod's refinement of nature .is apparent throughout- the work, a refinement which, here, as in almost all his • sacred and dramatic compositions, seems - to. he hovering between mysticism and volupluoit.iness. This contrast of opposing ,prineiplee lends to his .writings a fascinsting intere-t both film a musical and a psychological point of view. In the Majestic treatment of the " Credo ' and of " Sanctue," we 1 recognise the mystic,whilst in the rich and soothing melodies of the" Kyrie" and the" Gloria? the more sensuous characteristice of the composer's nataire predominate. The choral portions of the mass are closely woven into the fabric of the work, and it is difficult to speak of them 'except as part of the ensemble. The attack. of chorus was vigorous' and: pointed, and some of the unison passages for the whole ef the voices both -forte and pianissimo, left little to he striven for. In congratulating the Society upon the fact that the orchestra was very largely made up of our local muesiciane, epecial mention is due to be made of the excellent performance of the reed instruments as a whole, the oboe obligato to the bass tole in the " Gl7iia " being especially worthy of note. The principal vocal parts were undertaken by Miss liubi-Newcombe, Mr. Alfred Jordan, and Mr. Stanley Cookson, end hoth jointly and severally, this trio sang with excellent taste and judgment. The ";t incarnatus " was a treat in tne way of subdued chanting, and in this and the various other concerted and soli passages throughout the mass, these artistes chewed themselves fully equal to its exigencies. Haydn's " Farewell" Symphony was undertaken by•the orchestra in the second:•part of the peogramme and—performed as it was With the paraphernalia of lighted candles and with the details of a darkened room and a quiet exit as each ' part came to a close—the effect was very quaint, and the audience was loud in its demonstrations of approval. .Miss Ilubi-Newcombe sang two songs, in neither of which she appeared -at her best, We • have hitherto associated this young and promising I • ' centatrice wit h the brilliant vocalisation of seine bravura operatic number in which she undoubtedly gives evidence of talent of no mean order. But conditioned by the more prosaic possibilities of the concert ballad—even when that is so superior as is Cowen's "Promise of Life "—both the immaturity of , her powers and some faults in voice production and training are apparent. _ Miss Newcombe may, how- ever, take courage. ' Thera is yet plenty of time in which to learn the art by which art is concealed, and, in some region of the wide field open to one destined for the vocal profession, she will eventu- ally—by dint of pains and perseverance—take a very creditable place. Mr. Stanley Cookson and Mr. Alfred Jordan had eech.a love-song of a high order of merit to sing. Both the "Bedouin Love- song" (l'insuti) and "The Devout Lover' (M. V. White) are excellent in their way, and in saying that the interpretation of both these songs, by the gentletnen named, was in every respect adequate and. musicianly, we shall be understood to be giving no grudging [need of praise. _ Tosti's." My Dreams' and Bordesi's Sacred Scena "'David singing before Saul "subsequently sung by Mr. Jordan and Mr. Ceokson respectively, were squally pleasing, and, had time permitted, an encore would clearly have been insisted upon by a delighted audience. The chorus and orchestra, performed the accompanied parie-songs " Daybreak " . (Eaton Failing). and " Break ! Break I": (Dr. Hiles) in an able and fin- ished manner. The latter especially was an alto- gether fine performance, and; as such, may be regarded as a fitting recognition and reminder of the composer's long and honourable connection with the Society. Mr. Crossley played the pianoforte : accompaniments to the various songs.

div.head: CIIILDRENS' MUSICAL PLAY Ar WARRINGTON.
div.p: CIIILDRENS' MUSICAL PLAY Ar WARRINGTON.

A number of the scholars of St. James' Church Schools, Latchford, gave a public performance on Wednesday evening, of "Examination Day" a children's musical play, the joint production of Messrs. F. Booth, and Mr. W. R. Stansfield, school- mater. The thbme of the play is very appropriate for a performance given in connection with a pub- lic It deals with the misfortunes of a school inspector, who misses his train from London to carry on the examination of 4 country school. His servant, who is inure fortunate in securing a seat in the " modern ignorr of time and tide," carries out the examination on his own account. He has just con- cluded operations, however, when the belated inspector makes his appearance miseh to the bewilderment of the schoolmistress, and to the confusion of the presumptuous valet. The three, however, consent, in song, to main- tain a " mumness " as the illegality of the examination; the mistress because she might lose the grant ; the in- spector because he might lose his office, and the servant because he might lose his master. During the noway- ing of this very short story, there are introduced among other things, the peculiarities of a school inspeetor—ap- pareetly with a local application—and the misfortunes of the sleepy boy of the school. As a performance for school children, the play is an exceedingly meritorious one, and shocld only require putting on the" market to ensure it success. The iibretta, which is the joint work of the collaboratorseis race and pleasant, and the songs sparkle with quaint fuu ; whilst here and there a touch of irony, where the capacities of school inspectors coca in for notice, is revealed. The music, which is com- posed by Mr.Booth,is "eatehy" and quaint,and in many places is delightfully reminiscent of the peculiar airs which are a cnaracteristic of Gilbert and Sullivan's comic operas. The children had been rehearsed with considerable thorouelmsse, and throughout deserved the generous approbation which was bestowed upon them by a large audience. In the examina- tion held by the inspector's servant, the children a,ct the trial' scene from " the Merchant of Venice," and in this give some creß ahie specimeas of elocution. The charaeters,which wen, " made up." with quite pro- ieesiotial finish were Louisa White (Portia),A. E. Richard- sen ;Antonio); Gilbert Knight (Bassanio) John Roberts (Snylosk), and Thomas Clerk@ (the Duke). Besides this anothetexaminatien teet,a number et' the boys (mom- of the Boys' Brigade),went througk several physical and military evolutions, with a promptness and preci- sion which spoke highly for their drilling. The choruses and part songs .were given with commendable accur- ars, in unison, and the soloists throughou: deserve much praise, both for the confideace and the excellent voices which they breught to hear on the work. "'hey weie i—ller Majesty's Inspector of Schools (Msjer Twigg). John Livingston ;- H. M. Inspector's Man-ser- vant. Fred Foulkes ; Sehoot Mistress,Margaret Kilesten; School AteendanceOfficer,Thenses Taylor ; A Doll Sleepy Boy, H. tikelhern. Teachers, Dunces, Scholars, &t. Alto- gether, the performance was a high tieeimony to !he work of M-ssrs. Booth and Stansfield, and there is no doubt that " Examination Day." when presented under conditions a little more favourable, will gain popularity in the sphere to which it, as a class of musical work, belones. The performance, as will be seen from an ad- vertismsnt on another page, will be repeated next Wed- nesday evening.

div.p: ODDFELLOWSRIP AT WARRINGTON

Hamblett has been a member of the Constitu- tion Lodge for upwards of twelve .years, and has held office for eight years, and has three times been elected N.G. District Treasurer P.G. Wadsworth.in making the presentation, said he hoped P.G. Humblett would not accept tha.; emblem as a kind of payment for hie services to the lodge, but as a mark of esteetn from the members. He trusted the ' presentation wools) stir young members up to take office in their lodge. By so doing they would be conferring both a benefit on the lodge and on them- selves. P.O. Hamblett briefly returned thanks. P.(. If. Taylor (secretary), in proposing a vote of thanks to P.G. Wadsworth for making the presenta- tion, referred in eulogistic terms to the conduct of Hamblen in attending to his duties during his term of office. No N.G. had ever performed his duties in a more satisfactory manner. The °floe was one which every young man ought to be proud to oecuny. P.G. Watson (treasurer) seconded the vote of thanks, which was carried amidst applause.

div.head: " GOOD FRIDAY" 1N- A LONDON: P.0:1(.
div.p: " GOOD FRIDAY" 1N- A LONDON: P.0:1(.
H E sTA !WING CHILDREN.

Mr. G. R. Sims, in his role of" ttagonet "in the " Referee " so prone to eiternating strides with tar, that it is dillieult to know wives retake him seriously. Yet few people e.ould have had little doubt. as to hii eatnestwas of purpose whenAhey read the following psragraph in his ".Mustard and Gress " gossip contri- buted to Sunday's issue of the " 11,feree :"-- I spent my Good Friday in the park watching the e'-il- dr4o at play, and I don't think I ever saw so many tiny mites all holiday-making entirely "on their own" before. There [A ere groups of ten or a dozen ragged little ones, many o Oyu, st arcely able to toddle, and the chief of .the party was in most instances young lady of some seven or eight SUmmers. About four o'c,ork under the trees and against the fences, some of the little party sat down to a frugal meal of milk and water and broad and butter. The milk and water was in an old lemonade bottle, out of which each child had a sip in turn, and the bread and butter was tied up in a ragged pocket- handkerchief, But all the little arties did not go in for light refreshment. I noticed as Istood and watched the proceedings many a pair of hungry eyes looking out of famished little faces at the bread and butter of the for- tunate ones. There is a tremendous amount of hunger still among the children of our mighty city, and sotne- how or other the park seems to be the place to which the starving children most resort. Many a time lately have I seen little girls, with tartored brothers and sist,irs clin7ing to their torn skirts, wr.tehing the feeding of the ducks with is look that 1 understood. I asked one little stepmother—doorstep mother—the other morning what she was thinking about, and she told me. She was wish- ing that someone would feed her little brothers and sisters instead of the ducks. Her little flack, she told me, had had no breakfast that day. and nothing the day before taut some bread a neighbour ha] given her. The father was in bed with rheumatics, lwr mother vat ill, and her brother out of work. I ask' d her, f don't know why, if her father was a Gladstoniae. " I don't know," she said. '6 What piper does he talo, ?" "0, anytbing-7-" The Sun " is general I reads to 'on." "And what part of the paper does he like best ?" "Oh, he allers asks me to read ';m polerticks and serciety." I thought of the sick workman with his starving family revelling in the details of " poriticv and socie:y," But that Is another story.

div.head: WARRINGTON SCHOOL OF ART.
div.p: THE WARRINGTON SCHOOL OF ART.
EXHIBITION OF STUDENTS' WORK.

An aspect somewhat different from that of pre- vious exhibitions, characterised the display of School of Art students' work, which has been held during the lastthree days at the Museum. Formerlly in addition to the work which was prepared for the examiners at Kensington, there was, a pleasing dis- play of paintings to be seen. The absence of this feature in tlici present exhibition, however, is attributable to two or three causes. Almost the whole of the advanced students, who kept together the Sketching Club—from whence these paintings , chiefly came—have severed their connection with the institution ; or as in the case of the three holders of the scholarships, gone to prosecute their studies else- -‘here. This, of course; from a public point of view, detracted somewhat from the exhibition ; but at the same time it should be remembered by those who regret the absence of pleasing pictures, that there was a dis- play of students' work' more comprehensive arid of a higher standard than has been seen at any previous exhibition. So that, while at first sight the work ap- peared to have deteriorated, it had, in reality, made a very significant advance. Certainly the present danger of the Sketching Club sinking •cut of existence is to be regretted, and an attempt ought to be made to revive such an excellent department of theinstitution ; but at .the same time, the students are under greater examina- tion pressure since their amalgamation with the Techni- cal Institute, and too much cannot be expected of them. A striking -feature of the display was the hanging of work executed at the Jullien Studio, Paris, by the three local holdsrs of the Laneashire scholarships, namely Messrs. Garside, Woodier, and Dooley. , There was a number of drawings from life models by these studeets. The work was rxecutecl in three half days. This is in accordance with the rules of a monthly competition at the studios, where- the work is examined by 'a professor, and the productions worthy of marks of merit selected. We were pleased to note that Mr. J. W. Dooley had three specimens which had been selected for the compe- tition, sod which obtained honourable mention. Two .4f Mr. 0. Gareide's specimens had also been selected,a.nd in addition to these be sent a study of an Italian girl, in oil, which seas full of expression and life. Several excel- lently executed studies from life similar to those of Mr. Menleffe were sent: by Mr. Woodier. With the work of these three students Mr. Aylward, the Master of the. School of Art, is extremely pleased, and considers they have all three, a more than average chance of , making progress in the artistic world. What few paint- ings there were on view were not-of more than ordinary value. Miss Chrimee submitted a fruit &imposition, and two studies of heads, which were thoroughly executed in- detail, though, perhaps, slightly lacking in animation. From Miss Ellen Cooper's brush there was a study of a head from the cast, which was executed with feeling both in tone and colour ; whilst from Miss Spinks • were two flower compositions which had no doubt been satis- facttir,ly treated. This year a great deal has been at- tempted in modelling, a department which has not been made much of hitherto. Very creditable specimens from life-sized models in antique have been the result, and they record an unmistakable advance in work of the right character. Some inconvenience, however, has been experienced in this department owing to the lack of a proper classroem, and wore of a high class character cannot he looked for until this difficulty has been removed and sufficient space given for the proper treatment of the large castes which are used. There was also some credits tile work in reliefs from-antiques,. &c.,which com- pered very favourably with last year's productions. From Mr. John Millard there wore some paintings from the mosaic, which were conspicuously clean in execution and very tasteful in design. In tile pattern,- Herbert Pierpoint showed a rather notable exhibit, with photo- graphic illustrations of the diverse patterns to which the design could be turned. There was some artistically executed ornamentation painting from Stanley Pierpoint, from whose brush also, were the only holiday sketches in the exhibition. These were hung in three frames and were specimens of good taritee as well as being ably treated. .Taken as a whole, the work of the etudonts, especiellk in modelling, compared well with the speci- mens which had been awarded Marks of merit last year, some of .which were hung in the same room. In this -direction ample proof was afforded of the fact that the school is reaching a higher Wane in the quality of its work, io.nd this is no doubt the outcome of efforts .made .:by Mr. Aylward, wh a, in the face of the increasing , stipulations which emanate from the different authori- ties, has produced results alike highly creditable to the Institution and to -the town. The scholarships taken. by Warrington last year sufficiently demonstrated that fact, Mr. *Aylward, as well as the Technical Instruction Committee are entitled to a generous meed Of support from all who are in sympathy with art education in War- rington. The work submitted by the candidates for art class teachers and masters certificates promises to be superior to that even of last year ; and as a matter of fact, the increased demands of the examiners renders this essential. A noticeable feature of the exhibition was a display of excellent specimens of decorative needle work, the work ef members of a ladies class under the, tuition of Miss Laverock.

div.head: WARRINGTON AND THE PARISH COUNCILS BILL.
div.p: WARRINGTON AND THE PARISH COUNCILS BILL.

At the meeting of the II arrinkton Board of Guar- dians held on Wednesday at th Workhouse, Mr. Ratcliffe in the chair, a discussion took place with reference ta the effect of the Local Government Act on Warrington. After con3ideration f the circular letter by this Clerk of the Lancashire County Council ol March 17th, 1894, it was resolved to reply to such letter as follows :-1. That no alteration he made in the num- ber of guardians and rural district councillers to be elected for each parish within this union except as fol- lows : That in each urban district divided into wards one guardian be elected for each ward, and that in each Parish formed from the extra municipal parts of the borough ot Warrington one guardian be elected. 2. That it is desirable to add so much of the hamlet of Orford as is without the municipal borough of Warring- ton to the parish of Winerick-with-Flulme and that such parish be called " Winwick-with-flulme Orford," .and that two guardians be elected for that parish. '3. That it is undesirable t divide any rural parish within this union into wards. 4. That the guardians and rural district councillors retire,as at present.simultaneously at the eat of each triennial period. It was futher resolved to re- commend that so much of the parish of Latchford as is without the municipal borough be added to such borough so that the whole of such parish may be in one sanitary district and in one administrative county, or failing the practicability of such addition, that such extra munici- pal part be a separate parish, and that in either case one guardian or rural district councillor be elected for same, and one guardian for Latchford Ward within the borough. That so much of the parish of Warrington as in south and south-west of the municipal borough, expect the Gate Wharf Farm, be added to the borough, so ier to be in one sanitary district, and that the Gate Wharf Farm be added to the parish of Great Sankey-, or failing the pieicticatality of such addition to the borough that the whole of such extra municipal part, inclusive of the Gate Wharf Farm,be a separate parish,to be called " Little Sankey," and that in either case one guardian be elected for SM.'. That any financial adjustment that - may be deemed equitable by reason Of the inclusion o f either of the extra municipal parts with the municipal boroagh be arranged with the Borough Council prior thereto. That. it is undesirabte to make any alteration, other than as above suggested, in the area of the district of the Warrington Rural Sanitary • Authority, and that, if practicahle, the Joint Committee be recommended to provide accordingly. That no alteration of the area of the Warrington Union ought in any case to be made, and in the event of any such alteration being proposed. that the Guardians of this Union be heard thereon., That tiie Guardians further recommend that the num-- ber of Parish Councillors to be fixed for each rural parish in this union, unless otherwise desired at a parish meet- lime, be limil al to five. Mr. W. J. SilaW and Mr. A. J. Jolley each expressed themselves in favour of the members of the urban town- ships (Warrington, Newton, and Elaydock) being elected en bloc, a s at present, and Mr. Shaw moved a resolution to this effect.—The Clerk however, pointed out tort it would be far better to have wards, especially from a financial point of view, for in that case when an extra candidate came forward, or in a bye-election, the whole • township would not be put to the expense and treuble of ah election. An election covering the whole of the , township would entail the expense of about £lOO. On the other hand, if the townships were divided into wards, the expense would be greatly diminished, for elections might only lel ke place in one of the two wards, while the rest would not be contested. The expenditure would therefore be proportionately less. Anether point in favour of the ward system was that the municipal elections in Warrington, which township would be princi- pally affected by the motion, would take place on Nov. Ist, and the district council elections upon Nov. 8-h. The whole electoral machinery would therefore be to hand for use again. Again, the voting for the district councillors would then be by ballot, and not by papers taken round on which the elector put his initials against the person he voted for. It would be unfair that a .nien should have to go to the ballot box, and have to dOde perhaps omit of twenty names whom to vote for.—After further elucidation by the Clerk, Mr. Shaw's motion fell through, and upon the scheme being put to the meeting for approval, only Mr. A. J. Jolley voted against it.

THE TREES IN lIIGU-STREET, NEWTON:

-- Sir,—l am sure the trees in our High-st., make a charming addition to the scenery of the district, and therefore I am all the more surprised to find that although they are occasionally destroyed or they die, yet the Commissioners have not replaced those which have gone. The expense is not much, so perhaps it is an oversight that it has not boen done. Will our " new Commissioner" think of us P—Yours truly, R. W. STUART. Laurel Bank, Newton-le-Willows.

div.head: SUGGESTION.
div.p: A SUGGESTION.

Sir,—Whilst strolling through the town the other even- ing, I noticed in a shop window a valuable silver cup presented by Percy Davies, Esq., to he competed for by our junior Rugby football teams. Going a little fur- ther I discovered another valuable cup in another window to be competed for by the local Association football teams. It is needless to say that I am heartily glad to see that we have such benevolent and influential donors encour- aging our local teams, and fully appreciate their gener- osity; but we have another institution in Warrington which deserves recognition in some such way, and which is of far greater value to members of the community than any (of the above, and which has, indeed, been likened to the National Lifeboat Institution, for the saving of human life, and. giving help and rendering first aid to the injured. I refer to the local corps of the St. John Ambulance Association. I think if some of our respected fellow- townsmen (especially those whO are large employers of labour), would subscribe towards a cup to be competed for by members of the Warrington Centre, it would give a great impetus to ti.e movement,and by uoing so would be the means of alleviating a great deal of the pain and suffering which arises from the many accidents and cases ot sudden illness which occur. Trusting you will give this letter a space in your valuable paper,and apolo- gising to you for any trouble.—l remain yours. faithfully PROGRESSION. Warrington, April, 1894.

div.head: STATE OF THE STREETS.
div.p: THE STATE OF THE STREETS.

Sir,—l wonder if you can help me out of a difficulty. I am one of those who "want to know, you know," who is responsible for the intAligent way in which our public streets and roads are watered. Is the " man on the box" told off from head quarters to do it every day in the week,at this season of the year, wet or fine, or is he t)ld off from the same- source not to do it, wet or fine? I am sure, from the way in which it is done, that I. for one, can't tell how it is done. During the nights of Mon- day and Tuesday We bad copious showers of rain ; the streets on the following mornings were quite damp and refreshing to look at, not a particle of dry dust to be seen, and yet here that man is, as I write on Wed- nesday morning, deluging the ground, footpath is well, and looking at it quite affectionately,as if he were think- ing that he was doing it" a world of good." Now if I were a town fcoundrel, (Oh dear ! I mean Councillor) or a J.P.,and just stepping out, on my way to business. that man would jump off his seat and turn the tap, (or whatever it is,) and stop the flow of water beautifully, rather than run the risk of splashinc, my boots or pants; or if I were a cyclist, I should slip desperately through it, or have to dismount, consoling myself. certainly, b.( indulging in a few •' swear words" suitable to the occa- sion, (a thing I never, " well, hardly ever "do,) but as I am neither, I suppose I must wade through it as best I can; but if that man turns round and gives it another dose, (and by Jove ! be is doing,) I shall certainly have to consider the practicability or otherwise, of going to business in a boat.—Yours, " Warrington, April Ch.

div.head: TOWN CLOCK.
div.p: THE TOWN CLOCK.

Sir,—The noble science of Astronomy is the grand guide and corrective of horology; which again is the handmaid of the higher science. Now the methods by which " The Heavenly science " has been brought to its present state of perfection are precisely those in which your correspondent, F.W.R. , is so conspicuously lacking. The astronomer aims at the utmost possible accuracy, while acknowledging that this can only be approxim- ately attained. Again, he is ever willing to accept cor- rection, both as to methods and results, but never takes this as a personal affront when offered. Only by such means—t,ee, open and candid criticism—can approxim- ate truth be mere closely attained. And the man who complains of such criticism as bbing " personal re- marks "simply endorses and makes the fallacies his eoin. It is amusing to have Gritrithorpe's " Clocks, watches, and Bells " referred to and seemingly recommended te me ! My copy (1874) is nEarly worn out—seen much service ! But nowhere do I find it recommending a shaky suspension in place of solid masonry. Every clock—turret or other—should have the firmest possible suspension. Ns mere bolted iron work can in this respect compete with the mass of good solid masonry. Hear what Grimthorpe himself has to say on this— " Whatever increases the art without increasing the weight (of the pendulum) is obviously a great advan- tage ; and the principal things which do that, are dim- inution of triction and inertia of the train, and steadi- ness of suspension ot the pendulum. Even smaller pen- dulums generally incresse their arc from about 2 degs. in the factory to 2 degs 30 recs.as soon as they are proper- ly fixed to a good wall on stone corbels or iron beams," these last of course resting and bedded on solid stone Finally let me recommend a new experienceto Mr. Reynolds. Let him write to .Lord Griinthorpe stating the points in dispute. From what I know ot the epistolary style of his krdseip, I predict a reply very salutary if not very satisfactory to F.W.R.—Trulv yours, JO UN PEERS.

FRODSHAM VESTRY. Sir,—As the public can see that free speech is prac- tically prohibited, and discussion dreaded, as may be inferred from what Mr. Charles Reynolds said (possibly unintentionally) kindly allow me to place before your readers a few facts, and I leave them to judge as to whether "there is perfect harmony and peace in the parish" as the Vicar stated. On the 20th February last at the Disestabiishintnt meeting held here, a letter was read from a residen,', Non.conformist minister stating: " That the religious instruction given in their Sabbath schools was upset by the teaching given in the church day schools." From two Nonconformist pulpits on one Sabbath complaiets were made as to the teaclOng given by one of the curates : " That it was wrong to go to chapel, because the word chapel was not in the New TestameLt, but the word church was." 'This same curate has told people "that Nonconformist ministers could do no good because the bishop had not laid hands upon them, but he ttiie curate) could trace his pedigree back to the apostles." Of course he owns his pedigree comes from a very unwelcome—warm source, e7ery time he and his friends sing hymn 352 v. 2, compared with John

6c. 70v. _ Was there peace in the parish after a speech by Bishop Jayne on education, when the bishop's retnarks were publicly and severely censured at a public meeting held in Five Crosses Wesleyan Chapel the following evening? Is there harmony inside the church, when tour out of every six persons decline to stand during processions of singers and clergy? AU honour to them. What is the result of all this Ritualism ? It drives the men away from the church. Why, sir, on 21 Feb. last, at a Fpecially adverti*etlsermon in the Iron Church, special preacher, the audience corn posed only two males, exclusive of parsons and officials, and on Easter .Sunday morning at the Parish Church the audience was seven females to one male. I nstice that about nine-tenths of the different vestries are not held on Bank Holiday, and that the churckes where the gospel is faithfully preached the greatest amount of real good work is being accomplished, and tier- is no Ida of funds, even wit h- out having to retort to doubt fill ways of rai4ing money, Truth will bear diset:s.sian. t'ell interest makes cowards of mast men.—Yours truly. M,Froisham, April 2, 1894.
ROBERT FOULKES.
THE SOCIALISTIC PA.I';ACEA.

Sir,—Like certain patent medicines, Socialism is now loudly advertised as the cure-all for every disease of the body politic. Moral and social wooden legs and oblique vision disappear with magical celerity before this modern nostrum remedium. Truly its effects are marvell- ous on paper, and in the dreams of its promoters. Ac- cording to these enthusiasts, its universal. use and adoption would cleanse the world now stricken with moral leprosy. It this be so, by all means let the remedy be applied—the disease is evident and, if it has been properly dietnosed, and Socialism is the remedy indicated—why,then, let us have it. But—but is it? Are there no causes, besides individualism and competi- tion which many have been largely contributive to the production of the serious evils we see around us ? I have no panacea tor these evils. They,heing the results of many contributory causes, will require, at least as many different remedies to remove them. The old, old Confucian maxim," Do as ye would be done by," might go a long way towards this " consummation de- voutly to be wished "—if we would only adopt the pre- scription and i.apply the remedy. But in the mean- tie? Well, while we are waiting for men to become suffi- ciently alive to their own best interests and Oft, rights and claims of others. I propose that the Socialists demon- trate the validity of their views and the entire practic-

ability of their schemes by colonizing some unsetticd land. At present they propose to graft their Socialism upon the individualistic stock. After individualism has, so to speak, cleared the ground, the tocialist proposes to step in and reap the benefit of the exertions of the other and then turn round upon him and exclaim— " Ecce Signum." Now the question is. would Socialism stand the test of this isolation and colonization? Has it sufficient vitality to strike root and thrive indepen- dently of the individualistic stock? If the world could only prevail upon itself to spare the Socialists for a ' season whil3 this experimentunt crucis was performed— if the poor individualists could get along with- out them, some very valuable results would accrue. Chief among these would be the great blessing of less noise, for it would give the quietus to what is now merely a noisy controversy. In view of this latter fact it would be well if most of the colonists were deaf and took over with them a good supply of cotton wool and competent aurists. In pleasing prospect if this reign of "peace on (this part of) earth," I am truly yours, JOHN PEERS.
