RUGBY FOOTBALL.

The Warringtonia—n-s—icave been trying for some years past to lower the colours of the Widnes club at Widnes, but have failed in every attempt, although generally the score has been very small against them. The same ill- luck has followed them again this season, for on Satur- day they,were defeated by a try tl nil. Now that the league matches are over, there has been less interest taken in the doings of the various teams. The Widnes match however always excites a great amount of in- terest, owing to the proximity of the two towns to each other. It was therefore strange that there was not a larger " gate."

Warrington have not had their full strength during recent matches.. In the Widris match there was only eight regular players who had taken part in the league games.. It is pretty evident with so many absentees, the Warrington combination would be considerably at sea. The Widnesians however are to be complimented on their good play, especially forward, where they had the better of their opponents to a marked dPgree.

The day was more favourable for cricket than for football, as the broiling sun was very fatiguing to the players, and made them to lax their exertions. There, are inw only three more weeks after to-day before the close of the football season, and the hard-worked players would no doubt welcome the prospect of four mouths' rest before the next season commences. Warrington have still one Ar two stiff contests before them Wore the season ends for they have to meet Stockport who defeated them in the early part of the season, and they have also the two St. Helens clubs. They have, there- fore, their work cut out for the next week or two. _

The " A "teams shared the fate of their seniors on Saturday, and it is a long time since both firAt and" A" team were beaten on the same date. The "A " team is not near so strong as it used to bP, but Saturday's defeat was not a disgrace, for it was only the cleverness of the goal kicker which gave Widnes the victory. The first team's requirements had weakened the " A team considerably. and this scarcity of players is another evidence of the near approach of the cricket season.

By the way, admirers of old clubs have now cause to don their" condensers," and crape, for one of the oldest teams in the north is no more. It is say the "Athletic News" with the deepest unfeigned regret that we record the untimely demise of the Mossley Football Club. Born young some years ago, the organisation in its infancy thrived wonderfully in the pure and balmy air of the luzley heights. When it could toddle along it was fired with ambition to see the sights of various cities, but the pace was too fast for the exchequer, as various member of the body were worn out, and it became difficult to replace them. Short of funds, short of vitality, and short of all that makes a club healthy, it joined the competition, and after a very hard struggle to ke,tp on its legs, it has at last collapsed. It is now dead, leaving a noble baud of mourners and a few debts. R.I.P.

An accident cut short Mr. Biirrup's career as a player many years ago, thotigh he still, as a hale old :.:gentleman of seventy-three, takes a keen interest in the game. It was he who first started Anglo-Australian matches. He went down to Liverpool to see the first team off—earlri in the fifties, advanced one hundred and fifty pounds apiece for their expenses, and settled with a bailiffs' man, who camedown just as the ship was starting with a writ for the arrest at one of the best players, without whom the trip would probably have been a failure.

The widow stated that de- ceased had been in poor health for some months past, but had resumed his work since Christmas. He rose on Tuesday morning a little after seven, and before going to work told witness to tell him when she came to the shop if their son Alfred had got up. When she went to the shop she told him that she had left the son in bed. Deceased then left the shop, went to the house, and soon afterwards his body was found in the dam. 'fliey were poor, and deceased and witness had to work co hard as they could. They would be better off if Alfred would work, but he had been idling for a week or two.—Wm. Kilvert, a lad from Manchester, John Taylor, Rosh Green, and sergeant Wynne gave evidence of finding the bode. The coat and waistcoat were folded, and placed together on the hank along with dm cap.—The jury returned a verdict of " ;aikido whilst temporarily iasane."

That information , should have been given to the magistrates and it would have pieced a different complexion entirely upon the matter. If they were to be eternally frustrated as they had been, it would not be a question of the Beard to find ancommodation for 100 children, but rat her for 1,509 or 1,600. It would boa very serius thing if they had to take such steps throne) the hostility of the mana- gers of schools from whom they had a right tc expect that the school visitort should be treated with c-vility, . and should be assisted in accomplishing a difficult task. The Clerk explained, that the master was summoned hoping that he would be able to prove the boy had not been refused. He was the Board's witness, and there- fore it was not for the officer to try to prove that lie was incorrect. —Mr. Imison wished to know if the woman stated before the Committee that she had tried to eet the boy into the school or not P—Mrs. Handley: Yes.— Mr. Imison t And did the officer try to ascertain the correctness of that statement.—Mr. Handley : Yes.— Mr. Imison : Then it seems to ins to be fatal. If the prosecution was taken it was a natural defeness.—Mr. Handley : We wanted an explanation. At this juncture Mr. Bowyer, the school attendance officer, was called in- to the room and questioned with regard to the matter. Replying to Dr. l'lcDotleall,lir said he nad acted accord- ing, to the instructions of the Committee. Be informed the Committee otthe result of his inquirieseind that the boy had been refused. On several previous eccasions similar statements had been made, but on Atria inves- tigation-had been found to be incorrect. With regard to the case under discussion he did not get the information from Mr. Annett as to the refusal. He (Mr. Bowyer) had on previous occasions obtained written statements which he had proved to the Bench, and some of those cases were distnissed.—Dr. McDougall thought that the matter now rested with the Committee.—Canon Wood said that tie understood that Mr. Moss had written to Mr. Aneett on the subject in the most courteous manner. —The Clerk intimated that the difficulty was of long standing and he wished to be spared from going into it fullv.—Canon Wood said the subject. would be made pub- lic and if an explanation were not given it would appear that the Board had acted with discourtesy. The Board had acted,he thoughtswith extreme courtesy.—The Clerk I then entered fully into explanation.—Dr. McDougall said ' the public were given to understand that If the Board had communicated with the schoolmaster he would have given his reasons for not admitting the boy. The clerk had treated the.manegers with the utmost consideration, but it appeared to he a want of caution to take a sum- enons out before sufficient information had been gained. 1, —Canon Wood : The alternative of • summoning., is to leave the matter alone.—Dr. McDougall remarked that he had spoken to .a competent master upon the • matter in Runcorn and he replied that he would have • taken the boy in and made the best of him.— Canon Wood said that this was what the master should have done. The Committee had not the power to make him do that which lie objected to. It rested with the mana- gers of the school. It was an ill-iudged precedent on the master's part and brought voluntary schools into disrepute in the town.—Dr. McDougall : It is a terrible mistake..—The discussion then closed. -EVENING CLASSES. , Mr. Moss said it was the usual practice to vote £5 for the prize fund connected with the evening classes. Miss Kilburn desired to have a few awards for those girls at- tending classes.—Dr. McDougall proposed and Mr. Imi- son seconded that £6 be voted.—This was agreed to. • INCREASED PRECEPTS. The Clerk stated that the preempt for the last half year was £320. There had been several sources of increased expenditure which would necessitate over £4OO during the present six months.—On the proposition of Mr. Handley seconded by Dr. McDougall a call was made Tor £4OO.

TUN RUINATION OF TIM BLIND.

The Clerk reported that in Runcorn there were four blind children under the age of sixteen and one deaf and dumb boy. The duty of the Board was to provide elementary education for these children and the most suitable place for them to acquire this was at the school in Hardman-at. Liverpool. The mute being a Roman Catholic could he sent to St. John's Deaf ,and Dumb In- stitution at Boston Spa, Lancashire. The parent was lis,ble to contribute towards the child's expense. He had obtained information, and the subject might be referred to the School Attendance Cenunittee with instructions to make all necessary arrangements and report to the Board. Mr. Lake as appointed solicitor to the Board.

div.head: PRIMUOIE LBAGUE BALL.
div.p: PRIMUOIE LBAGUE BALL.

On Vonday evening a ball in connection with the Warrington Habitation (No. 1469) of the Prim- rose league was held in the Assembly Room of the Conservative Club, when about 100 ladies and gen- tlenien were present. Mrs. Reynolds the ruling councillor was unable to be present tl.rough indis- position. Dancing commenced at eight o'clock to music supplied by Mr. R. H. Pearson's well-known band, and was kept up until about two o'clock on the following morning. Mr. George Riley officiated M.C., while the duties of hon. treasurer were discharged by Mr. Louis A. Voisey, and those of hon. secretary by Mr. C. if. Wood.

Before I took the Norton Arms Hotel, Messrs. For nearly three years Messrs.
